Why the Other Options Are Incorrect?

• A. Atenolol: Continue perioperatively. Abrupt withdrawal of β-blockers can precipitate rebound hypertension, tachycardia, and myocardial ischemia.
• B. Furosemide (Lasix): Generally continued in patients who require ongoing volume control, although the morning dose may be withheld in selected patients to avoid hypovolemia or electrolyte disturbances depending on clinical status.
• D. Aspirin: Low-dose aspirin is often continued in patients taking it for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease, unless the surgery carries a high bleeding risk (e.g., intracranial or posterior eye surgery). For laparoscopic cholecystectomy, continuation may be appropriate after balancing bleeding and thrombotic risks.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman is scheduled for elective craniotomy for excision of a frontal lobe tumor. The anesthesiologist plans to use Total Intravenous Anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol and remifentanil to optimize intraoperative cerebral physiology. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of TIVA?
options: It increases the risk of renal toxicity
It increases the risk of malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It reduces cerebral metabolic rate

• Total Intravenous Anesthesia (TIVA) commonly employs propofol, often in combination with remifentanil. Propofol reduces cerebral metabolic rate (CMR), cerebral blood flow (CBF), and intracranial pressure (ICP) while maintaining good cerebral autoregulation. These properties make TIVA particularly useful in neurosurgical procedures and in patients with raised intracranial pressure.
• Additionally, TIVA provides rapid recovery, stable hemodynamics, and a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting, making it well suited for both neurosurgical and ambulatory surgery.

Other Options:

• Option A. It increases the risk of renal toxicity: Incorrect. Propofol is extensively metabolized by the liver, with additional extrahepatic metabolism. It does not produce clinically significant renal toxicity.
• Option C. It increases the risk of malignant hyperthermia: Incorrect. Propofol is not a trigger for malignant hyperthermia and is the preferred induction agent in susceptible patients.
• Option D. It inhibits hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: Incorrect. Inhibition of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is mainly associated with volatile inhalational anesthetics. TIVA has minimal effect on this protective pulmonary mechanism.

Educational Objective:

• TIVA with propofol decreases cerebral metabolic rate, cerebral blood flow, and intracranial pressure, making it the anesthetic technique of choice for many neurosurgical procedures.
• It also provides rapid recovery, hemodynamic stability, and is safe in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman is scheduled for elective laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia. During the pre-anesthetic discussion, a junior resident reviews the factors that influence the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) of inhalational anesthetics. The consultant points out that one of the statements is incorrect. Which of the following statements regarding MAC is incorrect?
options: MAC is a measure of the potency of an inhalational anesthetic.
MAC values are lower in females than in males.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MAC values are lower in females than in males.

• Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) is the alveolar concentration of an inhalational anesthetic required to prevent movement in 50% of patients in response to a surgical stimulus. It is the standard measure of the potency of volatile anesthetic agents—a lower MAC indicates a more potent anesthetic.
• Although several physiological and pharmacological factors influence MAC, sex does not. Healthy males and females have similar MAC values.

Other Options:

• Option A. MAC is a measure of anesthetic potency of an inhalational anesthetic: Correct. MAC is inversely related to anesthetic potency; agents with a lower MAC are more potent.
• Option C. Acute alcohol use decreases MAC: Correct. Acute ethanol intoxication reduces anesthetic requirements, whereas chronic alcohol consumption increases MAC due to enzyme induction and tolerance.
• Option D. Hyperthermia increases MAC: Correct. Hyperthermia (particularly temperatures >42°C) increases anesthetic requirements, whereas hypothermia decreases MAC.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 46-year-old patient is being mechanically ventilated for acute respiratory distress syndrome. The ventilator settings are: tidal volume 480ml, frequency 25 breaths per minute, PEEP of 5cm of H20, and FiO2 of 90%. His weight is 60 kg. Arterial blood gases are normal. Which of the following can be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decrease tidal volume

In ARDS, the cornerstone of management is lung-protective ventilation to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury. The recommended tidal volume is \~6 mL/kg of predicted body weight. For a 60-kg patient, this equals \~360 mL, but the patient is receiving 480 mL (≈8 mL/kg), which increases the risk of volutrauma and barotrauma despite normal ABGs. Hence, tidal volume should be reduced first.

Why others are incorrect:

• Option A: FiO₂ can be reduced later, but lung protection takes priority.
• Option C: Lowering RR risks hypercapnia.
• Option D: PEEP is already minimal; reducing it may worsen oxygenation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman develops fever, jaundice, and marked elevation of liver enzymes several days after receiving halothane anesthesia for surgery. Investigations suggest halothane-induced hepatitis. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this complication?
options: Immune complex deposition within hepatic sinusoids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypersensitivity to trifluoroacetyl (TFA)-modified hepatic proteins

Halothane undergoes oxidative metabolism, generating trifluoroacetyl (TFA) metabolites that bind to hepatic proteins. These altered proteins act as neoantigens, triggering an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that can result in fulminant hepatitis.

Educational Objective:

Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction caused by antibodies directed against TFA-modified liver proteins formed during oxidative metabolism of halothane.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 48-year-old male with a history of severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and a body mass index (BMI) of 45 presents for an emergency exploratory laparoscopy for an incarcerated inguinal hernia. He undergoes an uncomplicated induction and placement of an oral endotracheal tube via video laryngoscopy. The ideal volatile anesthetic for maintenance would be?
options: A volatile anesthetic with analgesic properties should be used to limit the amount of opioids required for the patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The least soluble volatile anesthetic

In a morbidly obese patient with severe OSA, the ideal volatile agent is one with low blood–gas and fat–blood solubility, such as desflurane.

• Low solubility allows rapid titration, faster emergence, and quicker recovery of airway reflexes, which is crucial in OSA to reduce postoperative airway obstruction and hypoventilation.
• Highly soluble or lipophilic agents accumulate in adipose tissue, causing delayed emergence and prolonged respiratory depression.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Most lipophilic agent: Accumulates in fat → delayed recovery.

Option C- Analgesic volatile: Volatiles have minimal true analgesia.

Option D-Highly metabolized agent: Increases metabolic burden without benefit.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with CKD is scheduled for surgery. Her serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL and eGFR is 13. Which of the following opioids can be safely used in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Remifentanil

• Remifentanil is the safest opioid in severe CKD because it is metabolized by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases.
• Not dependent on renal or hepatic function.
• It has an ultra-short acting, with no active metabolites, so accumulation does not occur even with very low eGFR.
• Hence, it is ideal for patients with advanced renal failure.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Pethidine forms normeperidine, a neurotoxic metabolite that accumulates in renal failure.

Option C: Alfentanil undergoes hepatic metabolism with reduced clearance in CKD.

Option D: Morphine produces M6G and M3G, which accumulate and cause respiratory depression and neurotoxicity.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension is scheduled for an elective open cholecystectomy. His only regular medication is amlodipine 5 mg once daily. During the pre-anesthetic evaluation, he asks whether he should take his morning antihypertensive medication on the day of surgery. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Omit amlodipine on the morning of surgery
Continue amlodipine at a reduced dose
Continue amlodipine at the usual dose
Substitute amlodipine with enalapril before surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue amlodipine at the usual dose

Calcium channel blockers, including amlodipine, should generally be continued throughout the perioperative period, including on the day of surgery. Unlike ACE inhibitors and ARBs, they are not routinely withheld because they are less likely to cause refractory intraoperative hypotension.

Educational Objective:

Most antihypertensive medications are continued before surgery. The main exceptions are ACE inhibitors and ARBs, which are usually withheld on the morning of elective surgery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy lasting 90 minutes under general anaesthesia, maintained with 65% nitrous oxide, oxygen and sevoflurane. At the end of surgery, the anaesthetic gases are discontinued, neuromuscular blockade is fully reversed (ToF ratio 0.95), and she is extubated breathing room air. She is awake, obeying commands, with a respiratory rate of 15/min and good chest expansion. Within 3 minutes, SpO₂ falls from 99% to 85%. The chest is clear, there is no stridor and no airway obstruction. Which mechanism best explains this desaturation?
options: Passage of nitrous oxide from the alveoli into the pulmonary circulation, reducing alveolar volume
Residual neuromuscular blockade causing hypoventilation and alveolar hypoxia
Uptake of sevoflurane into blood owing to its high blood:gas partition coefficient
Passage of nitrous oxide from the pulmonary circulation into the alveoli, diluting alveolar oxygen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Passage of nitrous oxide from the pulmonary circulation into the alveoli, diluting alveolar oxygen

Diffusion hypoxia (Fink effect)

| Step | Event

| ---- | -----

| 1 | N₂O discontinued → steep partial pressure gradient from blood to alveolus

| 2 | Rapid diffusion of N₂O from the pulmonary circulation into the alveoli

| 3 | ↑ Alveolar volume

| 4 | Dilution of alveolar O₂ (↓ concentration)

| 5 | Hypoxia

| Treatment | O₂ supplementation

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine is scheduled for an elective inguinal hernia repair. During the pre-anesthetic evaluation, she asks whether she should stop her thyroid medication before surgery. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop the drug 24 hours before surgery
Stop the drug one week before surgery
Stop the drug 5 days before surgery
Continue the medication on the day of surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continue the medication on the day of surgery

Levothyroxine should be continued throughout the perioperative period, including on the day of surgery. Abrupt discontinuation is unnecessary because of its long half-life and may worsen hypothyroidism.

Educational Objective:

Thyroxine replacement therapy should not be withheld before elective surgery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with a severe traumatic brain injury is undergoing emergency craniotomy for evacuation of an acute subdural hematoma. During induction of anesthesia, the anesthesiologist administers thiopentone to provide cerebral protection. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the cerebroprotective effect of thiopentone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased cerebral metabolic rate

• Thiopentone is a barbiturate that provides cerebral protection by markedly reducing the cerebral metabolic rate (CMR) and cerebral oxygen consumption (CMRO₂).
• The resulting decrease in metabolic demand is accompanied by reduced cerebral blood flow (CBF) and intracranial pressure (ICP), while preserving the coupling between cerebral metabolism and blood flow.
• By lowering the brain's oxygen requirements, thiopentone helps limit neuronal injury during focal cerebral ischemia, making it useful in selected neurosurgical and neurocritical care settings.

Other Options:

• Option B. Reduction of cerebral vasospasm: Incorrect. Thiopentone does not relieve cerebral vasospasm. In fact, accidental intra-arterial injection may provoke vasospasm because of its highly alkaline solution.
• Option C. Calcium channel blockade: Incorrect. Thiopentone acts primarily by enhancing GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission, not by blocking calcium channels.
• Option D. Free radical scavenging: Incorrect. Thiopentone does not exert its neuroprotective effect through antioxidant or free radical scavenging activity.

Educational Objective:

• Thiopentone protects the brain by decreasing cerebral metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, thereby reducing cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure while lowering neuronal oxygen demand during periods of cerebral ischemia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is being managed in the ICU. The intensivist decides to implement Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) in his ventilatory support. Which of the following statements about PEEP is incorrect?
options: Useful in situations where PO2 is low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreases intracranial tension (ICT)

PEEP is widely used in ARDS to improve oxygenation by preventing alveolar collapse and increasing functional residual capacity, hence it is useful when PaO₂ is low. By improving alveolar recruitment, PEEP can also enhance CO₂ elimination in some patients. However, PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and may impair renal perfusion and function. Importantly, raised intrathoracic pressure impedes cerebral venous drainage, leading to a rise in intracranial pressure, not a decrease.

Why others are correct:

• A. Useful in hypoxemia – True
• B. May help CO₂ clearance – True
• C. Can impair renal function – True

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 58-year-old male has a drug-eluting stent placed 10 months back and currently on dual antiplatelet therapy. When should this anti-platelets be stopped before the current elective surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Need not to be stopped

In a patient with a drug-eluting stent placed 10 months ago, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) should not be stopped for elective surgery. Current guidelines recommend continuing DAPT for at least 12 months after DES placement, as premature discontinuation significantly increases the risk of acute stent thrombosis, which carries high mortality. Elective surgeries should ideally be postponed until completion of 12 months of DAPT. If surgery is unavoidable, cardiology consultation is mandatory, and continuation of antiplatelets is preferred unless bleeding risk is life-threatening.

Why others are incorrect:

• A & B: Early cessation markedly increases thrombosis risk.
• C: One day is inadequate for platelet recovery and unsafe.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 58-year-old male with community-acquired pneumonia is intubated. Latest ABG on current ventilator settings: • Mode: Volume assist-control • VT: 6 mL/kg PBW • RR: 14/min • FiO₂: 0.50 • PEEP: 8 cmH₂O ABG: • pH: 7.21 • PaCO₂: 60 mmHg • PaO₂: 82 mmHg • HCO₃⁻: 24 mEq/L Breath stacking or dynamic hyperinflation is not observed. Which ventilator adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Decrease FiO₂ to 0.30 and increase PEEP to 12 cmH₂O
Add bicarbonate infusion to correct the acidosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase respiratory rate to 22–26/min

• This patient has primary respiratory acidosis:

• ↓ pH (7.21)
• ↑ PaCO₂ (60 mmHg)
• Normal HCO₃⁻ → acute ventilatory failure

→ The problem is inadequate alveolar ventilation, not oxygenation.

• Alveolar ventilation (V̇A) determines PaCO₂
• It is proportional to:

• Respiratory rate (RR)
• Tidal volume (VT)

But in lung-protective ventilation (ARDS/ pneumonia):

• VT is kept low (≈6 mL/kg PBW) to prevent volutrauma
• Therefore, PaCO₂ is best controlled by adjusting RR
• Increase respiratory rate → ↑ minute ventilation → ↓ PaCO₂ → correct acidosis

Why not other options:

A. Increase tidal volume (8–10 mL/kg):

• Violates lung-protective strategy
• ↑ risk of barotrauma/volutrauma

C. Change FiO₂/PEEP:

• Addresses oxygenation (PaO₂), which is already acceptable (82 mmHg)
• Does not correct hypercapnia

D. Bicarbonate infusion:

• Treats metabolic acidosis, not respiratory cause
• May worsen CO₂ load (→ CO₂ generation)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history is scheduled for an elective colectomy. During the pre-anesthetic evaluation, the anesthesiologist counsels him about the physiological effects of chronic smoking and the benefits of smoking cessation before surgery. Which of the following statements regarding the effects of chronic smoking is incorrect?
options: Elevated nicotine levels increase sympathetic activity.
Increased carboxyhaemoglobin causes a rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve.
Impaired mucociliary clearance and reduced surfactant production contribute to decreased pulmonary function.
Smoking increases the risk of postoperative infections by impairing immune function.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased carboxyhaemoglobin causes a rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve.

• Chronic smoking increases carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) levels because carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin with a much higher affinity than oxygen. This not only reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood but also causes a leftward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, making hemoglobin hold onto oxygen more tightly and reducing oxygen delivery to tissues.
• Smoking cessation for as little as 12 hours before surgery lowers carboxyhaemoglobin levels, improving tissue oxygenation.

Other Options:

• Option A. Elevated nicotine levels increase sympathetic activity: Correct. Nicotine stimulates catecholamine release, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and the risk of perioperative arrhythmias.
• Option C. Impaired mucociliary clearance and reduced surfactant production contribute to decreased pulmonary function: Correct. Smoking damages ciliary function, increases mucus production, and impairs surfactant activity, predisposing patients to atelectasis and postoperative pulmonary complications.
• Option D. Smoking increases the risk of postoperative infections by impairing immune function: Correct. Smoking adversely affects neutrophil and macrophage function, delays wound healing, and increases the risk of surgical site and pulmonary infections.

Educational Objective:

• In chronic smokers, carbon monoxide increases carboxyhaemoglobin levels, producing a leftward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve and impairing oxygen delivery.
• Smoking also increases sympathetic activity, impairs pulmonary defense mechanisms, and suppresses immune function, all of which contribute to increased perioperative morbidity.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with ASA Physical Status III is evaluated before elective abdominal surgery. Pulmonary function tests are performed after bronchodilator therapy to assess operative risk. Which of the following spirometry findings indicates moderate airflow obstruction requiring further pulmonary evaluation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FEV₁ <0.80 L and FEV₁/FVC <0.70

An FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction. When associated with an FEV₁ below 0.8 L, it suggests significant pulmonary impairment warranting further preoperative evaluation.

Educational Objective:

Patients with FEV₁ <0.8 L and FEV₁/FVC <0.70 are at increased perioperative pulmonary risk and require optimization before surgery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is scheduled for an elective inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia. During the pre-anesthetic visit, the parents ask how long the child should remain fasting before surgery. Which of the following fasting recommendations is correct for children older than one year?
options: Clear liquids – 2 hours; light meal – 6 hours; fatty meal – 8 hours
Clear liquids – 4 hours; light meal – 6 hours; fatty meal – 8 hours
Clear liquids – 2 hours; breast milk – 2 hours; solids – 4 hours
Clear liquids – 6 hours; light meal – 8 hours; fatty meal – 10 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clear liquids – 2 hours; light meal – 6 hours; fatty meal – 8 hours

Current fasting guidelines recommend:

• Clear liquids: 2 hours
• Breast milk: 4 hours (infants)
• Infant formula/light meal/non-human milk: 6 hours
• Fatty meal: 8 hours

These recommendations reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration while minimizing dehydration and patient discomfort.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient has grade III ASA. Which of the following post bronchodilator PFT findings requires further evaluation of the lung function of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FEV1 < 0.8 and FEV1/FVC <0.7

Post-bronchodilator pulmonary function tests are used to identify persistent (fixed) airflow obstruction that warrants further evaluation and perioperative risk stratification. An FEV₁/FVC <0.7 confirms obstructive lung disease, and an FEV₁ <80% predicted indicates at least moderate functional impairment, which is clinically significant in an ASA III patient. This combination suggests reduced pulmonary reserve and increased risk of postoperative pulmonary complications, thus requiring further assessment and optimization.

Why others are incorrect:

• FEV₁ <0.85 cut-off is too high and may represent mild or normal variation.
• FEV₁/FVC <0.75–0.8 does not meet the standard diagnostic threshold for obstruction.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60-year-old man undergoes elective surgery under general anesthesia. Following endotracheal intubation, spontaneous respiration fails to return for several hours after completion of the procedure. He remains apneic despite adequate reversal of anesthesia. Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly reduced plasma pseudocholinesterase activity, and genetic testing demonstrates an atypical pseudocholinesterase enzyme with reduced affinity for its substrate. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is most likely responsible for this patient's prolonged apnea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mivacurium

• This patient has atypical (deficient) plasma pseudocholinesterase, resulting in impaired metabolism of certain neuromuscular blockers.
• Mivacurium is a short-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker that is hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase. In patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency, its metabolism is markedly delayed, leading to prolonged neuromuscular blockade and apnea.

Note: Succinylcholine is the classic drug associated with prolonged apnea due to pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Since it is not listed among the options, mivacurium is the correct answer.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Pancuronium

• Long-acting nondepolarizing blocker
• Eliminated mainly by the kidneys
• Not dependent on plasma pseudocholinesterase

B. Rocuronium

• Intermediate-acting aminosteroid
• Primarily eliminated via the liver
• Reversal possible with sugammadex

D. Atracurium

• Undergoes Hofmann elimination and nonspecific ester hydrolysis
• Independent of pseudocholinesterase activity
• Preferred in renal and hepatic failure

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60-year-old obese male is scheduled for elective surgery under general anesthesia. He has a history of obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, and a BMI of 35. Preoperative airway assessment is performed to determine if the patient has a difficult airway, as this could complicate the intubation process during the surgery. Based on the clinical tests, which of the following findings would classify this patient as having a "difficult airway”?
options: Upper lip bite test: Ability to protrude mandible
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mallampati score III

A Mallampati score III indicates that only the soft palate and base of the uvula are visible, which correlates with reduced oropharyngeal space and a higher likelihood of difficult laryngoscopy and intubation, especially in obese patients with OSA. This is a well-established predictor used in routine airway assessment.

Why others are incorrect:

Option B- Thyromental distance 7 cm: Normal (≥6.5 cm); suggests adequate mandibular space.

Option C- Sternomental distance 13 cm: Normal (>12.5 cm); indicates good neck extension.

Option D- Upper lip bite test (mandible protrusion): A positive test predicts easy, not difficult, intubation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 62-year-old male with septic shock and ARDS (PaO₂/FiO₂ = 120) is intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. His current ventilator settings are: • Mode: Volume assist-control • VT: 8 mL/kg predicted body weight • FiO₂: 0.80 • PEEP: 5 cmH₂O • RR: 22/min • Plateau pressure: 32 cmH₂O Despite these settings, his SpO₂ remains 88%. According to lung-protective ventilation strategies for ARDS, which of the following is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Increase VT to 10 mL/kg to improve oxygenation
Increase RR to 30/min without changing VT
Increase PEEP to 12–15 cmH₂O and reduce VT to 6 mL/kg
Switch to pressure support ventilation to reduce plateau pressures
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase PEEP to 12–15 cmH₂O and reduce VT to 6 mL/kg

Why C is correct

ARDS ventilation goals:

• Low tidal volume: 6 mL/kg
• Plateau pressure < 30 cmH₂O
• Higher PEEP for recruitment
• Accept permissive hypercapnia

Current plateau = 32 → high → VT must go ↓

Current PEEP = 5 → too low for severe ARDS

Other options:

• A. Increase VT to 10 mL/kg to improve oxygenation: Increase VT → increases barotrauma + worsens plateau pressures
• B. Increase RR to 30/min without changing VT: Increase RR only → oxygenation issue is not fixed + worsens hyperinflation
• D. Switch to pressure support ventilation to reduce plateau pressures: Switch to PSV → not used in acute ARDS (patient not ready to trigger ventilator)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with end-stage chronic kidney disease is scheduled for the creation of an arteriovenous fistula under general anesthesia. During the pre-anesthetic planning, the anesthesiologist avoids an analgesic that can produce a neurotoxic metabolite which accumulates in renal failure and may precipitate seizures. Which of the following anesthetic drugs is contraindicated in patients with chronic renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pethidine (Meperidine)

Pethidine (meperidine) is contraindicated in chronic renal failure because its active metabolite, norpethidine (normeperidine), is eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with impaired renal function, this metabolite accumulates and can cause central nervous system toxicity, including agitation, tremors, myoclonus, and seizures.

Other Options:

• Option A. Morphine: Incorrect. Morphine produces active metabolites that accumulate in renal impairment and may prolong sedation and respiratory depression. However, it is not absolutely contraindicated and may be used cautiously with dose reduction and close monitoring.
• Option B. Fentanyl: Incorrect. Fentanyl undergoes hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites and has minimal dependence on renal excretion, making it the preferred opioid in patients with renal failure.
• Option D. Atracurium: Incorrect. Atracurium is eliminated by Hofmann degradation and ester hydrolysis, processes that are independent of renal and hepatic function. Therefore, it is a preferred neuromuscular blocker in patients with renal impairment.

Educational Objective:

• In patients with chronic kidney disease, pethidine should be avoided because of the accumulation of its neurotoxic metabolite, norpethidine.
• Fentanyl and atracurium are preferred alternatives due to their organ-independent or minimally renal-dependent elimination and more predictable pharmacokinetics.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 64-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following major abdominal surgery. He requires light sedation while remaining easily arousable, cooperative during neurological assessment, and able to maintain spontaneous respiration. The intensivist selects a sedative that produces a state most similar to normal physiological sleep. Which of the following drugs best fulfills these requirements?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dexmedetomidine

Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α-adrenergic agonist that produces sedation closely resembling natural non-REM sleep. It acts primarily on the locus coeruleus, the brain's principal wakefulness center, resulting in a unique form of sedation in which patients are:

• Easily arousable and cooperative
• Able to maintain spontaneous ventilation
• Less likely to develop significant respiratory depression
• Returned to a sleep-like state when stimulation ceases

These properties make dexmedetomidine particularly useful for ICU sedation and procedural sedation requiring frequent neurological assessment.

Other Options:

• Option A. Propofol: Incorrect. Propofol produces deep GABA-mediated sedation that differs from physiological sleep and is associated with dose-dependent respiratory depression and apnea.
• Option B. Midazolam: Incorrect. Midazolam alters normal sleep architecture by suppressing deep and REM sleep and can cause respiratory depression, amnesia, and prolonged sedation.
• Option D. Ketamine: Incorrect. Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia, characterized by preserved airway reflexes but a cataleptic state with hallucinations and EEG patterns unlike normal sleep.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 65-year-old man suddenly collapses in the operating room. Cardiac monitoring shows an organized electrical rhythm at a rate of 60/min, but no palpable pulse is detected. The rhythm is diagnosed as pulseless electrical activity (PEA). What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: High-quality CPR with intravenous epinephrine while searching for reversible causes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High-quality CPR with intravenous epinephrine while searching for reversible causes

Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) is a non-shockable rhythm. The cornerstone of management is:

• Immediate high-quality CPR
• Epinephrine (1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes)
• Identification and treatment of reversible causes (5 Hs and 5 Ts)

Defibrillation has no role in PEA.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for an elective abdominal surgery. His regular medications include amlodipine, losartan, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and prednisolone. During the pre-anesthetic assessment, the anesthesiologist reviews which medications should be continued on the day of surgery. Which of the following drugs can be safely withheld on the day of surgery with minimal risk of adverse effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ACE inhibitors/Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are commonly withheld on the morning of elective surgery because they increase the risk of refractory intraoperative hypotension, particularly after induction of general anesthesia. Omitting a single dose is generally safe and does not significantly increase perioperative cardiovascular risk.

Other Options:

• Option A. Statins: Incorrect. Statins should be continued throughout the perioperative period because they reduce cardiovascular complications and provide vascular protective effects.
• Option B. Beta blockers: Incorrect. Patients already receiving beta blockers should continue therapy. Abrupt withdrawal may precipitate rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and myocardial ischemia.
• Option D. Steroids: Incorrect. Patients on chronic corticosteroid therapy should continue their usual dose and may require perioperative stress-dose steroids to prevent adrenal insufficiency.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease and reduced left ventricular function is scheduled for emergency laparotomy. The anesthesiologist chooses an induction agent that produces minimal changes in heart rate, blood pressure, and myocardial oxygen demand. Which intravenous induction agent is the best choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Etomidate

Etomidate is the most cardiovascularly stable intravenous induction agent. It produces minimal myocardial depression and preserves sympathetic tone and baroreceptor function, making it the preferred induction agent in patients with coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and hemodynamic instability.

Educational Objective:

Etomidate is the IV induction agent of choice in patients with compromised cardiovascular function because it preserves hemodynamic stability.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with end-stage renal disease is scheduled for elective surgery under general anesthesia. While planning intraoperative neuromuscular blockade, the anesthesiologist decides to avoid a muscle relaxant that is predominantly eliminated by the kidneys, as it may result in prolonged paralysis. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is primarily excreted via the renal route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pancuronium

Pancuronium is a long-acting, non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, with nearly 80–90% excreted unchanged in the urine. Consequently, its duration of action is significantly prolonged in patients with renal impairment, making it a poor choice in this setting.

Elimination of Common Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

| Muscle Relaxant | Duration | Primary Route of Elimination

| --------------- | -------- | ----------------------------

| Pancuronium | Long-acting | Renal (80–90%)

| Vecuronium | Intermediate | Hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion (major), partial renal excretion

| Atracurium | Intermediate | Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis (organ-independent)

| Rocuronium | Intermediate | Hepatic uptake and biliary excretion

Other Options:

• Option B. Vecuronium: Incorrect. It is eliminated mainly through hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion, with only a smaller proportion excreted by the kidneys.
• Option C. Atracurium: Incorrect. It undergoes Hofmann elimination, a spontaneous plasma degradation that is independent of renal and hepatic function, making it an excellent choice in renal failure.
• Option D. Rocuronium: Incorrect. Rocuronium is predominantly cleared by the liver and excreted in bile, with minimal renal elimination.

Educational Objective:

• Among commonly used non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, pancuronium is the most dependent on renal excretion and should generally be avoided in patients with significant renal dysfunction.
• Atracurium, because of its organ-independent Hofmann elimination, is the preferred agent in patients with renal or hepatic failure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 70 kg elderly athlete undergoes surgery and is administered succinylcholine due to the unavailability of vecuronium. A total of 640 mg of succinylcholine is given intermittently. During recovery, the patient is unable to breathe spontaneously or move limbs. What is the explanation?
options: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency increasing action of succinylcholine
Undiagnosed muscular dystrophy and muscular weakness
Muscular weakness due to fasciculation produced by succinylcholine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase 2 blockade produced by succinylcholine

A total dose of 640 mg succinylcholine in a 70-kg patient is excessive and can convert the usual phase I depolarizing block into a phase II (desensitizing) block. Phase II block resembles a non-depolarizing neuromuscular block, with flaccid paralysis, TOF fade, and prolonged apnea, explaining the inability to breathe or move during recovery.

Why others are incorrect:

• A. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency increasing action of succinylcholine: Causes prolonged block after normal doses, not massive cumulative dosing.
• C. Undiagnosed muscular dystrophy and muscular weakness: Would cause hyperkalemia and cardiac issues, not isolated prolonged paralysis.
• D. Muscular weakness due to fasciculations produced by succinylcholine: Cause transient myalgia, not prolonged apnea or paralysis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A baby is born through thick meconium-stained liquor. At birth, the baby has a weak cry, poor tone, and HR of 90 bpm. The attending resident proposes tracheal suctioning before PPV. The senior consultant intervenes. Which of the following correctly describes the management of this baby?
options: Tracheal suctioning must be performed first in all MSL babies before initiating PPV
Tracheal suctioning is recommended only in vigorous MSL babies before PPV
Initial steps followed by PPV; tracheal suctioning in non-vigorous babies is not recommended
Initial steps followed by PPV; tracheal suctioning is performed after HR improves to >100 bpm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Initial steps followed by PPV; tracheal suctioning in non-vigorous babies is not recommended

Resuscitation of Meconium Stained Liquor (MSL) Baby:

| Baby's condition | Management

| ---------------- | ----------

| Vigorous (strong cry, good tone, HR >100) | Initial steps → PPV if needed

| Non-vigorous (weak cry, poor tone, low HR) | Initial steps → PPV directly

| Tracheal suctioning in non-vigorous | Not recommended

Order of Resuscitation: Temperature → Airway → Breathing → Circulation

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A critically ill patient has been receiving propofol at 5 mg/kg/hour for 72 hours. He develops severe metabolic acidosis, refractory bradycardia, rhabdomyolysis, and hyperkalemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Propofol infusion syndrome

Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) is a rare but potentially fatal complication associated with high-dose (>4 mg/kg/hour), prolonged (>48 hours) propofol infusion. It is characterized by metabolic acidosis, refractory bradycardia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, cardiomyopathy, and acute cardiac failure.

Educational Objective:

PRIS results from mitochondrial dysfunction with impaired electron transport and fatty acid metabolism, leading to multiorgan failure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A firefighter with extensive thermal burns involving approximately 60% of his body undergoes emergency surgery several days after the injury. Shortly after induction of anesthesia, the ECG shows tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation, progressive widening of the QRS complex, and eventual merging of the QRS and T waves into a sine-wave pattern. He subsequently develops ventricular fibrillation followed by asystole. Which of the following drugs most likely caused this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Succinylcholine

The ECG changes indicate severe hyperkalemia:

• Tall, peaked T waves
• PR prolongation
• Widened QRS complex
• Sine-wave pattern
• Ventricular fibrillation and asystole

In patients with major burns, there is upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors across skeletal muscle membranes. Administration of succinylcholine, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, opens these receptors and causes massive potassium efflux from muscle cells.

This can produce sudden, life-threatening hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest.

Important timing

Succinylcholine is generally considered unsafe after the first 24–48 hours following a major burn, and the risk may persist for many months until receptor expression returns toward normal.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Atracurium

• Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker
• Does not cause significant potassium release
• May cause histamine release and hypotension

B. Baclofen

• GABA-B receptor agonist used for spasticity
• Does not cause acute hyperkalemia during anesthesia

C. Halothane

• Volatile anesthetic associated with hepatotoxicity and malignant hyperthermia
• Does not typically produce this classic hyperkalemic ECG sequence

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient presents with acute exacerbation of COPD and requires non-invasive ventilation. Which mode of ventilation is typically preferred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP)

In acute exacerbation of COPD, BiPAP is the preferred non-invasive ventilation mode because it provides two pressure levels: higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) to reduce work of breathing and improve CO₂ clearance, and lower expiratory pressure (EPAP) to prevent airway collapse. This directly addresses hypercapnic respiratory failure, reduces intubation rates, and improves survival.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A preterm neonate delivered at 28 weeks requires cord clamping. According to the 2025 key update, which of the following is the most appropriate step and its primary benefit in this infant?
options: Immediate cord clamping to allow rapid resuscitation
Delayed cord clamping for at least 60 seconds to reduce intraventricular haemorrhage
Milking of the umbilical cord as an equivalent alternative
Delayed cord clamping only if SpO2 is below 70% at 2 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Delayed cord clamping for at least 60 seconds to reduce intraventricular haemorrhage

Delayed cord clamping (≥60 sec) in preterm infants specifically reduces intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) by avoiding cerebral blood flow fluctuations, in addition to improving iron stores. The 2025 update emphasises this benefit particularly for preterms.

• Preterm infant (<37 weeks): Delay cord clamping for ≥60 seconds if vigorous.
• Major benefit in preterm infants: ↓ Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH).
• Additional benefits: ↓ Need for blood transfusion, ↓ NEC, ↑ Iron stores, improved circulatory stability.
• Cord milking: Avoid in infants <28 weeks because of increased risk of severe IVH.
• Immediate cord clamping: Only if immediate resuscitation or maternal instability mandates it.
• Term baby → DCC mainly improves iron stores.
• Preterm baby → DCC is tested for its reduction in IVH, NEC, and transfusion requirements.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A preterm neonate in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) requires elective endotracheal intubation for worsening respiratory distress. To minimize the risk of vagal-induced bradycardia, provide adequate analgesia, and facilitate intubation, the neonatal team plans premedication before the procedure. Which of the following is the recommended sequence of drug administration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atropine → Fentanyl → Vecuronium

Premedication for elective neonatal intubation aims to improve intubating conditions while minimizing physiological stress. The recommended sequence is:

1. Atropine – Administered first to prevent vagal-mediated bradycardia during laryngoscopy and airway manipulation.
2. Fentanyl – Given next to provide analgesia and blunting of the stress response to intubation.
3. Vecuronium – Administered last to achieve neuromuscular relaxation, facilitating smooth and atraumatic endotracheal intubation.

Giving a muscle relaxant only after adequate analgesia ensures the infant is not paralyzed while conscious.

Other Options:

• Option B. Fentanyl → Atropine → Vecuronium: Incorrect. Atropine should precede airway manipulation and opioid administration to reduce the risk of reflex bradycardia.
• Option C. Vecuronium → Fentanyl → Atropine: Incorrect. Administering a neuromuscular blocker before analgesia is inappropriate and leaves the infant paralyzed without adequate pain control.
• Option D. Atropine → Vecuronium → Fentanyl: Incorrect. Analgesia should be established before administering a neuromuscular blocking agent.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Activation of which receptor results in inhibition of ADH secretion and leads to diuresis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. κ-opioid receptor agonist

• Activation of κ-opioid receptors inhibits the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary, leading to diuresis.
• This effect is classically associated with κ-agonists, which reduce water reabsorption in the collecting ducts by lowering ADH levels.
• Clinically, this explains the increased urine output seen with certain opioids acting on κ receptors.
• κ-receptor (KOR) agonists inhibit ADH (vasopressin) release from the posterior pituitary → ↓ free water reabsorption → ↑ water diuresis. This is called: “κ-agonist induced aquaresis”.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: μ-opioid receptor agonists cause analgesia and respiratory depression, not ADH inhibition.

Option C: δ-opioid receptors are mainly involved in analgesia and mood modulation.

Option D: σ-receptors are not true opioid receptors and do not regulate ADH secretion.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: All are true about Propofol except:
options: It is an emulsion with egg lecithin present in it
It is considered the best agent for day care surgery
It is associated with high incidence of nausea and vomiting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is associated with high incidence of nausea and vomiting

• Propofol is well known for its antiemetic and antipruritic properties, making it highly favorable in anesthesia practice.
• It is formulated as a lipid emulsion containing egg lecithin, which allows intravenous administration.
• Because of its rapid onset, short duration of action, and smooth recovery profile, propofol is considered the agent of choice for day-care (ambulatory) surgery.
• Contrary to the statement, propofol is associated with a low incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) and is often used to reduce PONV risk.

Why others are correct:

Option A: Antipruritic – true

Option B: Egg lecithin emulsion – true

Option C: Ideal for day-care surgery – true

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: All of the following anaesthetic agents can be used in bronchial asthma except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiopentone

Thiopentone is not preferred in bronchial asthma because it can cause histamine release, leading to bronchospasm and increased airway resistance. This makes it unsafe in patients with reactive airways.

Why others are correct:

Option A- Halothane: Has bronchodilatory properties and suppresses airway reflexes, making it suitable in asthma.

Option B- Sevoflurane: A potent bronchodilator, non-pungent, and commonly used for induction and maintenance in asthmatics.

Option C- Propofol: Suppresses airway reflexes and has anti-bronchoconstrictive effects, making it safe and preferred for induction.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: All of the following are contraindications in IVRA except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mepivacaine

In IVRA (Bier’s block), mepivacaine can be used safely as it is an amide local anesthetic with a relatively favorable cardiovascular profile compared to bupivacaine. IVRA requires drugs with rapid onset and low cardiotoxicity.

Why others are contraindications:

Option A- Bupivacaine: Absolutely contraindicated due to severe cardiotoxicity if systemic leakage occurs.

Option B- Sickle cell anemia: Tourniquet-induced hypoxia and acidosis can precipitate sickling crisis.

Option C- Scleroderma: Associated with poor peripheral circulation, increasing risk of ischemic complications.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: All of the following are correct for Pediatric CPR except:
options: Use a cuffed endotracheal tube for intubating this child
Apply cricoid pressure during endotracheal intubation
Administer the initial dose of epinephrine within 5 minutes from the start of chest compressions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Apply cricoid pressure during endotracheal intubation

Routine cricoid pressure is not recommended during pediatric CPR or intubation. It can worsen the laryngoscopic view, delay intubation, and increase the risk of airway obstruction or hypoventilation. Current pediatric resuscitation guidelines advise against its routine use, especially in emergencies.

Why others are incorrect (they are correct statements):

• A. Administering 2 breaths every 2–3 seconds is appropriate once an advanced airway is in place.
• B. Using cuffed endotracheal tubes for intubating is safe and preferred in children when size and cuff pressure are appropriate.
• D. Administering initial dose of epinephrine within 5 minutes of starting chest compressions improves outcomes in pediatric cardiac arrest.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: All of the following can be given by intra-tracheal route except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. N-Acetyl cysteine

Only a limited group of emergency drugs can be administered via the intra-tracheal (ETT) route during resuscitation when IV/IO access is unavailable. These are remembered by the mnemonic NAVEL: Naloxone, Atropine, Vasopressin, Epinephrine, Lignocaine

N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) is not absorbed effectively through the tracheobronchial mucosa and has no role in intra-tracheal drug delivery, hence it cannot be given by this route.

Why others are incorrect (they CAN be given):

Option A- Epinephrine: Effective via ETT in cardiac arrest (higher dose required).

Option B- Atropine: Can be administered intratracheally in emergencies.

Option C- Naloxone: Lipid-soluble and absorbable through airway mucosa.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An elderly man with Ca pancreas is receiving intravenous opioids for pain management. Which of the following drugs can be safely administered to him because of ceiling effect on respiratory depression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Buprenorphine

Buprenorphine is a partial μ-opioid receptor agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, making it safer in elderly or frail patients receiving opioids for cancer pain.

Beyond a certain dose, further receptor activation does not significantly increase respiratory depression, reducing the risk of fatal hypoventilation while still providing effective analgesia.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Morphine is a full μ-agonist with dose-dependent respiratory depression.

Option C: Fentanyl is a potent full agonist and can cause profound respiratory depression.

Option D: Methadone has no ceiling effect and carries a high risk of respiratory depression and QT prolongation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario Pain Scale (CHEOPS) for rating postoperative pain includes all of the following, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oxygen saturation

The Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario Pain Scale (CHEOPS) is a pain assessment tool used to evaluate postoperative pain in young children who cannot reliably self-report.

It assesses behaviors including cry, facial expression, verbal response, torso position, touch, and legs.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Cry: Indicates distress and is a core CHEOPS component.

Option B- Legs: Position and movement reflect pain-related agitation.

Option C- Torso position: Assesses guarding or rigidity due to pain.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During cardiopulmonary resuscitation in an infant, the recommended depth of chest compressions is:
options: One-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. One-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest

Effective infant CPR requires chest compressions to a depth of approximately one-third of the chest diameter (about 4 cm or 1.5 inches) while maintaining a rate of 100–120 compressions/minute.

Educational Objective:

For infants, compress the chest at least one-third of its depth with complete chest recoil after every compression.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: ETCO₂ waveform shows elevated baseline with a progressively rising plateau. Which cause is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exhausted CO₂ absorber

Key sign: baseline fails to return to zero → CO₂ rebreathing.

• An elevated baseline with a progressively rising plateau on the ETCO₂ waveform indicates rebreathing of CO₂.
• Most commonly due to an exhausted CO₂ absorber in the anesthesia circuit.
• When soda lime is depleted, exhaled CO₂ is not adequately removed, causing inspired CO₂ to rise, reflected as an increased baseline and rising alveolar plateau.
• This is a classic capnography sign and requires immediate absorber replacement.

Why others are incorrect:

Option B: Excessive minute ventilation lowers ETCO₂, not raises baseline.

Option C: Esophageal intubation shows absent or rapidly declining ETCO₂.

Option D: Bronchospasm causes a “shark-fin” waveform, not baseline elevation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: For labor epidural analgesia, the ideal agent should demonstrate:
options: Dense motor block with minimal sensory block
Dense sensory block with minimal motor block
Pure motor block without sensory block
Pure sympathetic block without sensory block
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dense sensory block with minimal motor block

• For labor epidural analgesia, the goal is to provide effective pain relief from uterine contractions while preserving motor function so the mother can actively participate in labor and pushing.
• Hence, an ideal epidural produces a dense sensory block (T10–S5) with minimal motor blockade, typically achieved using dilute local anesthetic solutions (e.g., low-dose bupivacaine or ropivacaine with opioids).
• This improves maternal satisfaction and reduces instrumental delivery rates.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Dense motor block interferes with ambulation and effective pushing.

Option C: Pure motor block has no analgesic benefit.

Option D: Isolated sympathetic block does not provide adequate labor analgesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Gallamine is relatively contraindicated in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coronary artery disease

• Gallamine is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (curare-like drug) with a distinctive side effect profile. Gallamine has significant vagolytic (antimuscarinic) activity → Leads to tachycardia and increased cardiac workload
• In patients with Coronary artery disease:

• Tachycardia → ↑ myocardial oxygen demand
• Can precipitate angina or myocardial ischemia

Hence, relatively contraindicated in CAD

Why not other options:

A. Asthma:

• Gallamine has minimal histamine release
• Safer compared to agents like d-tubocurarine

B. Liver failure: Not primarily hepatically metabolized

C. Renal failure: Excreted by kidneys → may have prolonged action, but not the main contraindication tested

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: How long should elective surgery be deferred for a patient who was admitted in the ICU for severe respiratory infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 12 weeks

After a severe respiratory infection requiring ICU admission, elective surgery should be deferred for about 12 weeks.

Severe infections cause prolonged impairment of lung mechanics, gas exchange, respiratory muscle strength, and mucociliary clearance.

In addition, airway hyperreactivity and residual inflammation may persist for several weeks, significantly increasing the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications such as pneumonia, hypoxemia, reintubation, and prolonged ventilation.

Evidence shows that pulmonary risk normalizes closer to 3 months after severe lower respiratory tract infections.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- 6 weeks: Adequate only for mild infections.

Option B- 8–10 weeks: May still carry increased pulmonary risk after ICU illness.

Option D- 14 weeks: Longer than necessary without added benefit.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the defective enzyme in a patient whose dibucaine number was 20.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Butyrylcholinesterase

A dibucaine number of 20 indicates a severely abnormal pseudocholinesterase enzyme, consistent with butyrylcholinesterase (plasma cholinesterase) deficiency. Dibucaine normally inhibits this enzyme; low inhibition (normal ≈80, heterozygous ≈50–60, homozygous atypical ≈20) predicts prolonged apnea after succinylcholine or mivacurium due to impaired drug metabolism.

Why others are incorrect:

• A. Acetylcholinesterase: Acts at synapses; not measured by dibucaine test.
• B. Monoamine oxidase: Involved in neurotransmitter metabolism, unrelated to anesthesia drugs.
• C. Catechol-O-methyltransferase: Metabolizes catecholamines; no role in succinylcholine metabolism.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a child with difficult intravenous cannulation, an emergency intraosseous infusion is made through the tibia. What is the ideal site for inserting the needle in this tibial intraosseous infusion?
options: Below the tibial tuberosity at a 45° angle towards the epiphyseal plate
Below the tibial tuberosity at a 45° angle away from the epiphyseal plate
Above the tibial tuberosity at a 45° angle towards the epiphyseal plate
Above the tibial tuberosity at a 45° angle away from the epiphyseal plate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Below the tibial tuberosity at a 45° angle away from the epiphyseal plate

• The preferred site for tibial intraosseous access in infants and children is the proximal tibia, approximately 1–2 cm below the tibial tuberosity on the anteromedial surface.
• The needle is inserted at approximately 45° (or perpendicular depending on the device) and directed away from the proximal epiphyseal (growth) plate to avoid damage to the physis.
• The proximal tibia is preferred because it has a thin cortex, a broad medullary cavity, and is easily identifiable, making it ideal for rapid emergency vascular access.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient on mechanical ventilation and placed in prone position which of the following is true?
options: Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse
Increases venous return and thus maintains cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse

In mechanically ventilated patients, especially with ARDS, the prone position improves ventilation–perfusion matching by recruiting dorsal lung regions that are prone to collapse in the supine position. This prevents atelectasis and alveolar collapse, improves oxygenation, and reduces ventilator-induced lung injury by promoting more homogeneous lung inflation.

Why others are incorrect:

• Reduces CO₂ in alveoli: CO₂ clearance may improve, but this is not the primary or consistent effect.
• Decreases inspiratory pressure: Proning does not reliably lower airway pressures.
• Increases venous return: Prone positioning may actually reduce venous return due to increased intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Intense craving experienced by individuals recovering from chronic alcoholism can be treated with a drug that acts through which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Antagonist at opioid receptors

Intense craving in individuals recovering from chronic alcoholism is effectively treated with naltrexone, an opioid receptor antagonist.

• Alcohol increases endogenous opioid release, which enhances dopamine-mediated reward pathways.
• By blocking μ-opioid receptors, naltrexone reduces the reinforcing and pleasurable effects of alcohol, thereby decreasing craving and risk of relapse.
• It is commonly used as part of relapse-prevention therapy in alcohol dependence.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: β-adrenergic agonists have no role in alcohol craving control.

Option B: α-adrenergic agonists (e.g., clonidine) mainly reduce autonomic withdrawal symptoms.

Option C: Serotonin agonists are not primary anti-craving agents in alcoholism.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Major cause of perioperative hypothermia in neonates:
options: High surface area to body mass ratio
Excess evaporation due to renal losses
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High surface area to body mass ratio

Neonates are highly prone to perioperative hypothermia primarily due to a large surface area relative to body mass, which leads to rapid heat loss via radiation, convection, and conduction in the cold operating room environment. Additionally, thin skin, minimal subcutaneous fat, and immature thermoregulatory mechanisms worsen heat loss. Hence, meticulous thermal protection is essential during anesthesia and surgery.

Why others are incorrect:

• Option A: Neonates have limited shivering, but this is not the major cause of heat loss.
• Option C: Impaired sweating affects heat dissipation, not hypothermia risk.
• Option D: Renal losses do not significantly contribute to perioperative hypothermia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Neuroleptic anesthesia (also known as neuroleptanalgesia) is produced by combining which of the following agents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fentanyl + Droperidol + Nitrous oxide

• Droperidol = neuroleptic (antipsychotic)
• Fentanyl = potent opioid analgesic
• Nitrous oxide = added to enhance hypnosis & amnesia
•

This combination was historically sold as a fixed preparation:

•

Innovar = Fentanyl + Droperidol

Then N₂O was added during anesthesia → neurolept anesthesia

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Post-dural puncture headache depends on all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Timing of ambulation

Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is primarily related to CSF leakage through the dural hole, leading to intracranial hypotension.

•

Its incidence is strongly influenced by patient factors and technical factors, but early or delayed ambulation does not affect the risk of PDPH.

•

Studies have shown that prolonged bed rest after dural puncture does not reduce headache incidence, and early mobilisation is safe.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Younger age increases PDPH risk due to higher dural elasticity.

Option C: Pregnancy increases risk because of hormonal and anatomical factors.

Option D: Needle type (large gauge, cutting needles) significantly increases PDPH risk.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Preoperative fasting recommendation is
options: 2 hours for breast milk in infants
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 hours for liquids in adults

Current preoperative fasting (ASA) guidelines recommend that clear liquids (water, clear juice, black tea/coffee) may be taken up to 2 hours before anesthesia in adults.

This reduces dehydration, insulin resistance, and patient discomfort without increasing aspiration risk.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- 4 hours for solids in adults: Solid food requires at least 6 hours, not 4.

Option C- 2 hours for breast milk in infants: Breast milk requires 4 hours of fasting.

Option D- 4 hours for solids in infants: Infant formula/solids also require 6 hours, similar to adults.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Regarding opioids, all of the following statements are true except:
options: Sufentanil is the most potent clinically used opioid
Opioids decrease prolactin and increase LH hormone secretion
Methadone can cause QT interval prolongation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Opioids decrease prolactin and increase LH hormone secretion

Opioids actually:

• Increase prolactin
• Decrease LH
• Decrease testosterone
• Due to inhibition of hypothalamic GnRH pathways.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the recommended dose of adrenaline for a child during cardiac arrest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.01 mg/kg (1ml/kg of 1:10,000 solution)

During pediatric cardiac arrest, the recommended dose of adrenaline (epinephrine) is 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO, given as a 1:10,000 solution. Adrenaline improves coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure through α-adrenergic vasoconstriction and increases the likelihood of return of spontaneous circulation. This dose is repeated every 3–5 minutes during CPR as per PALS guidelines.

(Note: the correct volume is 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000.)

Why others are incorrect:

• 0.1 mg/kg (1:1000): Ten-fold overdose → severe arrhythmias.
• 0.001 mg/kg (1:100,000): Subtherapeutic and ineffective.
• 0.5 mg/kg: Grossly excessive and dangerous.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the recommended target preductal oxygen saturation (SpO₂) for neonates at 5 minutes after birth according to the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) 2025 guidelines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 80-85%

The Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) recognizes that healthy newborns do not achieve adult oxygen saturation levels immediately after birth. Oxygen saturation rises gradually over the first few minutes of life as the lungs expand and fetal circulation transitions to neonatal circulation.

Clinical Significance:

• Avoids unnecessary administration of excessive oxygen.
• Prevents hyperoxia-related oxidative injury, especially in preterm infants.
• Guides appropriate oxygen supplementation during neonatal resuscitation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which agent is most commonly used to achieve controlled hypotension during ENT/maxillofacial surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium nitroprusside

Controlled hypotension is intentionally induced during surgeries like ENT and maxillofacial procedures to:

• Reduce intraoperative bleeding
• Improve surgical field visibility
• Shorten operative time

Drug of Choice: Sodium nitroprusside (SNP) is most commonly used because:

• It is a potent, rapid-acting arterial and venous vasodilator
• Has immediate onset and short duration
• Allows precise titration of blood pressure

Why not other options:

A. Ketamine:

• Causes ↑ BP and HR (sympathomimetic)
• Opposite of desired effect

C. Etomidate:

• Used for induction of anesthesia
• Hemodynamically stable, does not produce hypotension

D. Phenylephrine:

• α₁ agonist → vasoconstriction → increases BP
• Used to treat hypotension, not induce it

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which among the following medications must be withheld on the day of surgery due to potential complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Furosemide

Furosemide, a loop diuretic, is commonly withheld on the day of surgery due to the risk of intravascular volume depletion, hypokalemia, and hypotension, which can worsen peri-induction hemodynamic instability and predispose to arrhythmias.

Electrolyte disturbances may also increase sensitivity to anesthetic drugs and neuromuscular blockers.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Digoxin: Usually continued to maintain rate control and cardiac function; stopping may precipitate arrhythmias.

Option B- Propylthiouracil: Must be continued to prevent perioperative thyrotoxicosis.

Option C- Prednisolone: Should not be stopped abruptly; stress-dose steroids may be required to prevent adrenal crisis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which inhalational agent is safe for a patient with Chronic Kidney Disease ( CKD ) on dialysis who is undergoing surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Desflurane

• Desflurane is the safest inhalational anesthetic in patients with CKD on dialysis because it undergoes minimal metabolism (<0.02%) and does not produce nephrotoxic fluoride ions or compound A.
• It is eliminated almost entirely via the lungs, making renal function irrelevant to its clearance.
• Hence, it is preferred when renal safety is a major concern.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Methoxyflurane: Causes high fluoride ion release → severe nephrotoxicity.

Option C- Enflurane: Undergoes hepatic metabolism with fluoride production → renal risk.

Option D- Sevoflurane: Can form compound A, which is potentially nephrotoxic, especially in low-flow anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is the preferred anaesthetic technique used in a surgery for a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. General anesthesia

In severe aortic stenosis, maintaining stable hemodynamics is critical. General anesthesia allows tight control over heart rate, preload, afterload, and contractility. Sudden decreases in systemic vascular resistance or preload can cause profound hypotension and myocardial ischemia, which are life-threatening in these patients. With GA, invasive monitoring and vasoactive support can be used to maintain coronary perfusion pressure and sinus rhythm.

Why others are incorrect:

• Option B: Spinal anesthesia causes abrupt sympathetic blockade and severe hypotension.
• Option C: Epidural anesthesia also risks vasodilation and reduced preload.
• Option D: Intercostal nerve block provides inadequate anesthesia for major surgery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which IV induction agent is associated with the highest incidence of post-induction apnea, especially in neonates and young infants?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Propofol

Propofol has:

• Rapid onset (due to high lipid solubility)
• Short duration (due to rapid redistribution)

Because of this fast CNS penetration, it causes:

• immediate depression of respiratory drive
• loss of airway reflexes
• reduced tidal volume + respiratory rate
• transient apnea post induction

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is an advantage of epidural over spinal anesthesia?
options: Duration can be prolonged using an inlaying catheter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duration can be prolonged using an inlaying catheter

A key advantage of epidural anesthesia over spinal anesthesia is the ability to prolong and titrate the duration of anesthesia and analgesia using an indwelling epidural catheter.

• This allows continuous or intermittent dosing, making epidural anesthesia ideal for long surgeries, postoperative analgesia, and labor pain control, with adjustable block height and intensity.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Less dose required: Spinal anesthesia requires a smaller drug dose due to direct CSF administration.

Option C- Easier technique: Spinal anesthesia is technically simpler and faster to perform.

Option D- Less traumatic needle: Spinal needles are finer and less traumatic than epidural needles.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is considered an absolute contraindication to spinal anesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patient refusal

Patient refusal is an absolute contraindication to spinal anesthesia. Relative contraindications include sepsis, severe spinal deformity, and pre-existing neurological disorders.

Educational Objective:

Absolute contraindications include patient refusal, coagulopathy, severe hypovolemia, raised intracranial pressure, infection at the puncture site, and severe aortic or mitral stenosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not weaning mode of ventilation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CMV

Continuous Mandatory Ventilation (CMV) is not a weaning mode because the ventilator delivers a fixed number of mandatory breaths regardless of patient effort, providing minimal opportunity for spontaneous breathing or respiratory muscle training. This can lead to diaphragmatic disuse and delays in liberation from the ventilator.

Why others are incorrect (they ARE weaning modes):

• SIMV: Allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory ones; mandatory rate can be gradually reduced.
• PSV: Supports spontaneous breaths with pressure assistance, promoting patient-driven ventilation.
• CPAP: Maintains airway patency while the patient breathes spontaneously, often used before extubation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence for CPR in Basic life support?
options: Assess the patient's response, Activate ERS, check carotid pulse, Start CPR
Check carotid pulse, Start CPR, call for help and activate ERS, Defibrillate
Defibrillate, assess response, check carotid pulse, Maintain airway
Start CPR, Activate ERS, Defibrillate, Check pulse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Assess the patient's response, Activate ERS, check carotid pulse, Start CPR

Basic Life Support (BLS) follows a systematic, time-sensitive sequence to rapidly identify cardiac arrest and initiate life-saving measures.

Correct Sequence (Adult BLS):

1. Assess responsiveness: Check for unresponsiveness (tap and shout)
2. Activate Emergency Response System (ERS): Call for help / code blue / EMS
3. Check pulse (carotid in adults) (≤10 seconds): If absent → cardiac arrest confirmed
4. Start CPR immediately: C-A-B sequence: Compressions first (30:2), then airway and breathing

Why not other options:

B. Check carotid pulse, Start CPR, call for help and activate ERS, Defibrillate: Starts with pulse check → delays recognition; wrong order

C. Defibrillate, assess response, check carotid pulse, Maintain airway: Defibrillation cannot precede assessment

D. Start CPR, Activate ERS, Defibrillate, Check pulse: CPR before assessment → inappropriate and unsafe

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following IV induction agents is associated with the highest risk of histamine release and cardiovascular depression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiopental

• Thiopental → causes histamine release → vasodilation → hypotension
• Effect is exaggerated in hypovolemic or shock patients
• Thiopental, a barbiturate, is most strongly associated with histamine release, leading to vasodilation, hypotension, and myocardial depression.
• It directly depresses cardiac contractility and reduces systemic vascular resistance, making cardiovascular collapse more likely, especially in hypovolemic or cardiac-compromised patients.
• Histamine-mediated effects can also cause bronchospasm and flushing.

Why others are incorrect:

• Option A: Propofol causes hypotension via vasodilation but has minimal histamine release.
• Option C: Ketamine is sympathomimetic, typically increasing heart rate and blood pressure.
• Option D: Etomidate is hemodynamically stable with negligible histamine release.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following LA would not need dose readjustment in a case of liver failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Procaine

• Procaine is an ester local anesthetic metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase, not by the liver.
• Therefore, its clearance is independent of hepatic function, and dose readjustment is not required in liver failure.
• This makes ester LAs safer than amide LAs in patients with significant hepatic impairment.

Why others are incorrect:

• A. Lidocaine: An amide LA extensively metabolized in the liver; reduced clearance in liver failure.
• C. Bupivacaine: Hepatic metabolism with high protein binding; risk of accumulation and cardiotoxicity.
• D. Ropivacaine: Also an amide LA requiring dose reduction due to liver-dependent metabolism.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following local anesthetic agents is commonly used for epidural analgesia during labor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bupivacaine

For labor epidurals we use long-acting amide LAs with good sensory block and minimal motor block, to allow pushing.

Common choices:

• Bupivacaine (most common)
• Ropivacaine (less motor block)
• Often combined with opioids (e.g., fentanyl or sufentanil) for synergy and dose reduction.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is classified as a long-acting non-depolarizing muscle relaxant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pancuronium

Pancuronium is a long-acting (>50 minutes) non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Rocuronium and atracurium are intermediate-acting, while mivacurium is short-acting.

Educational Objective:

Long-acting non-depolarizing muscle relaxants include pancuronium, doxacurium, and pipecuronium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following non-invasive investigations provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dobutamine stress echocardiography

Dobutamine stress echocardiography (DSE) is the most accurate non-invasive test for predicting perioperative cardiac complications.

It detects stress-induced wall-motion abnormalities, which directly reflect myocardial ischemia under physiologic stress similar to surgery.

A negative DSE has a high negative predictive value, making it especially valuable for perioperative risk stratification in patients unable to exercise.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A- Exercise ECG: Limited sensitivity and often not feasible perioperatively.

Option C- Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy: Useful but less specific for predicting perioperative events.

Option D- Coronary angiography: Invasive and anatomical; does not reliably predict perioperative risk.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements about sugammadex is false?
options: Sugammadex is a reversal agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.
Sugammadex does not reverses the effect of succinylcholine.
It is safe for use in patients with renal impairment
Side effects include tachycardia, blurring of vision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is safe for use in patients with renal impairment

Sugammadex is a selective relaxant binding agent that encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium, rapidly reversing neuromuscular blockade. It does not reverse succinylcholine, as it only binds aminosteroid neuromuscular blockers.
