However, sugammadex is primarily renally excreted, and in patients with severe renal impairment, the sugammadex–rocuronium complex may accumulate. Therefore, it is not considered safe or routinely recommended in significant renal failure.

Why others are correct:

• A. Sugammadex is a reversal agent for rocuronium and vecuronium: True. Reverses rocuronium and vecuronium.
• B. Sugammadex does not reverses the effect of succinylcholine: True. Does not reverse succinylcholine.
• C. Side effects include tachycardia, blurring of vision: Side effects may include cardiovascular and visual disturbances (though bradycardia is more common than tachycardia).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of these is the definition of effective CPR? 1. Respiratory rate: 20 - 24 breaths per minute. 2. Chest compressions: 100-120/min. 3. Allow complete chest recoil. 4. 2-2.4 inches depression.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3 and 4

Effective CPR is defined by delivering high-quality chest compressions that optimize perfusion. This includes a compression rate of 100–120/min, allowing complete chest recoil to permit venous return, and achieving an adequate depth of 2–2.4 inches (5–6 cm) in adults. These factors together determine coronary and cerebral perfusion during cardiac arrest.

Why the others are incorrect:

• 1: A respiratory rate of 20–24/min is not recommended during CPR; excessive ventilation reduces venous return and worsens outcomes.

Options including 1 are therefore incorrect.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While performing an interscalene block for shoulder surgery, the patient develops hoarseness of voice and difficulty speaking about 30 minutes after the block. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve block

Most common nerve to get blocked is phrenic nerve

• Hoarseness of voice and difficulty speaking after an interscalene block are classically due to ipsilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) blockade.
• Local anesthetic spread to the vagus nerve or RLN causes vocal cord paresis, leading to hoarseness, weak voice, and dysphonia.
• This is a known, usually transient complication of interscalene brachial plexus blocks.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Local anesthetic toxicity presents with CNS or cardiac symptoms, not isolated hoarseness.

Option B: Horner syndrome causes ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, not voice changes.

Option D: Phrenic nerve block causes diaphragmatic paralysis and dyspnea, not hoarseness.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While walking on the street, you find an unresponsive child. After confirming that the child is not breathing and there's no pulse, what is the next best course of action?
options: Deliver rescue breaths, as most pediatric cardiac arrests are secondary to breathing problems
Begin back blows and chest thrusts
Deliver 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths for 2 minutes, then leave the child to call for help
Leave the child immediately to search for an AED
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deliver 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths for 2 minutes, then leave the child to call for help

After confirming unresponsiveness and absence of breathing and pulse in a child, the next step is to initiate CPR immediately. In pediatric BLS, if you are alone, you should give 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, continuing CPR for about 2 minutes before leaving the child to call for help and activate EMS. Early CPR maintains cerebral and coronary perfusion and significantly improves outcomes in pediatric cardiac arrest.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: You are planning to wean a patient off mechanical ventilation. Which of the following is not a criterion to do so?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vital capacity more than 5 ml/kg

A vital capacity >5 mL/kg is not an accepted criterion for weaning from mechanical ventilation because it is too low to ensure adequate respiratory reserve.

Standard weaning parameters require a vital capacity ≥10–15 mL/kg, indicating sufficient inspiratory and expiratory muscle strength to sustain spontaneous breathing after extubation.

Why others are incorrect:

Option A: Tidal volume >5 mL/kg suggests adequate spontaneous breath size.

Option C: Minute ventilation <10 L/min reflects efficient ventilation without excessive work.

Option D: RSBI <105 is a strong predictor of successful weaning and extubation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 2-year-old child suddenly becomes unresponsive following a peanut ingestion. What is the next immediate step in management?
options: Intubate immediately with an endotracheal tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start chest compressions

A suddenly unresponsive child with suspected FBAO is treated as cardiac arrest. When a child becomes unresponsive, you immediately start the CPR sequence, beginning with chest compressions, not back blows or abdominal thrusts. Airway maneuvers are done only during CPR cycles.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60-year-old man collapses suddenly. He is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no pulse. Cardiac monitoring reveals a chaotic, disorganized rhythm with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves. After starting high-quality CPR, what is the next best step per ACLS protocol?
options: Deliver an unsynchronized shock at 120–200 J biphasic
Deliver an unsynchronized shock of 360 J
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deliver an unsynchronized shock at 120–200 J biphasic

Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm characterized by chaotic, disorganized ventricular electrical activity with no effective cardiac output. According to the American Heart Association (AHA) ACLS guidelines, the first intervention is immediate high-quality CPR and early defibrillation.

For a biphasic defibrillator, the recommended initial shock is 200 J (or the manufacturer’s recommended energy). Defibrillation is unsynchronized because there is no organized QRS complex to synchronize with.

Why not the other options?

| Option | Why it's wrong

| ------ | --------------

| A. Amiodarone | Reserved for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT — given after the second shock (per current AHA algorithm), not as the initial rhythm-directed intervention

| B. Synchronized cardioversion | Requires an organized QRS to sync to; VF has none, so the defibrillator may fail to discharge at all if synchronized mode is selected

| C. Unsynchronized shock at 120-200 J biphasic dose | Correct — VF is a shockable rhythm; defibrillation (unsynchronized) is the definitive treatment, given as soon as the rhythm is confirmed and the device is ready

| D. Unsynchronized shock of 360 J | Correct energy only for monophasic defibrillators; most modern devices are biphasic, using lower doses (120–200 J, per manufacturer)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A term neonate weighing 2 kg, delivered to a primigravida mother through vaginal route and through clear liquor, is found having gasping respiratory efforts after performing the initial steps in the delivery room. The next step in resuscitation is:
options: Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using 30% oxygen
Intubate and initiate positive pressure ventilation using 30% oxygen
Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using room air
Intubate and initiate positive pressure ventilation using room air
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using room air

• The neonate has gasping respirations after the initial steps of newborn resuscitation. Gasping is considered ineffective breathing, so positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) must be initiated immediately.
• For a term neonate, PPV is started with room air (21% oxygen).

Why not the other options?

• A. PPV with 30% oxygen: Incorrect. For term/late-preterm neonates, initial PPV is generally started with 21% oxygen.
• B. Intubation + 30% oxygen: Intubation is not routinely required as the first step; begin with bag-mask PPV.
• D. Intubation + room air: Although room air is appropriate initially, immediate intubation is not required unless bag-mask ventilation is ineffective or specific indications for intubation are present.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding resuscitation of a critically sick child?
options: Compression to ventilation ratio should be 30:2 with 2 rescuers
Chest compression depth should be one-third of A-P diameter of chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chest compression depth should be one-third of A-P diameter of chest

In pediatric resuscitation, effective chest compressions are critical and should be delivered to a depth of one-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest to ensure adequate cardiac output.

• Compression depth: one-third of chest A-P diameter (correct statement)

Compression–ventilation ratio:
• Single rescuer: 30:2
• Two rescuers: 15:2 (not 30:2)
• Preferred route for emergency drugs is IV; intraosseous is used when IV access is not available (not preferred primarily)
• Epinephrine IV/IO dose: 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg )
• Should be 1:10000, not 1:1000

Why other options are incorrect:

• IO is an alternative route, not the preferred first line if IV is available
• 30:2 ratio is for single rescuer, not two rescuers

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding High-Quality CPR?
options: Chest compression to Rescue breath ratio is 30:2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depth of compression must be 3-4cm

High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of at least 5 cm (about 2 inches) to generate adequate cardiac output. Recommended rate is 100–120/min with complete chest recoil between compressions.

| Parameter | Recommended Value

| --------- | -----------------

| Compression rate | 100–120/min

| Compression depth | 5–6 cm (2–2.4 inches)

| Compression : ventilation | 30 : 2

| Chest recoil | Must be complete

| Interruptions | <10 seconds

During chest recoil: Negative intrathoracic pressure develops

This allows:

• Venous blood to return to the heart
• Cardiac chambers to refill

If recoil is incomplete:

• Cardiac output decreases
• Coronary perfusion falls

The standard compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 for single rescuer CPR.

Thus, a depth of 3–4 cm is inadequate, making option D incorrect.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the management of patients who have achieved return of spontaneous circulation following CPR?
options: Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused
Perform emergent cardiac intervention if ST elevation is present in the ECG
Maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) above 65 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused

After successful CPR, the patient may develop Post–Cardiac Arrest Syndrome, which includes:

• Brain injury
• Myocardial dysfunction
• Systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury
• Persistent precipitating pathology (e.g., MI)

Immediate management focuses on oxygenation, circulation, neuroprotection, and treating the cause. Post–cardiac arrest care includes maintaining SpO₂ >94%, MAP ≥65 mmHg, and urgent coronary intervention if STEMI is present.

Current guidelines (AHA 2020 and the post-TTM2 trial era) recommend targeted temperature management between 32–36°C, with a strong shift toward simply maintaining normothermia and actively preventing fever (≤37.5°C). A target of "<33°C" is not the standard — aggressive hypothermia below 33°C showed no benefit over 36°C or fever prevention in major trials (TTM, TTM2). The underlying concept: after successful CPR, patients develop post-cardiac arrest syndrome — anoxic brain injury, myocardial stunning, systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury, plus the precipitating pathology. Management bundles target oxygenation (94%+), perfusion (MAP ≥65), temperature control (prevent fever; cool only if comatose), and treating the cause (e.g., PCI for STEMI).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of these are the components of high-quality CPR? a) Compression rate 100-120/min b) Depth of compression in adults is 3-4 cm c) Ventilation of 2 breaths for every 30 compressions d) Allow complete chest recoil
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. a, c & d

High-quality CPR requires a compression rate of 100–120/min, a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio, and complete chest recoil after each compression. The depth in adults should be 5–6 cm, so option b (3–4 cm) is incorrect; hence a, c & d are correct.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A smoker who was given an interscalene block for an arthroscopic acromioclavicular joint reconstruction 2 days ago was followed up by a Chest x-ray which showed as below. He is asymptomatic at present and is comfortably resting on the bed. What is the next step in management?
options: Insert chest drain as soon as possible
Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed

The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax.

As the patient is asymptomatic with no symptoms of dyspnoea or respiratory distress the best way to manage is to wait and watch.

Postoperative pneumothorax is seen mostly in patients with pre existing lung conditions like asthma or in chronic smokers. The pre-existing blebs or bullae in the individuals rupture due to pressure gradients created by the positive pressure from ventilation or the arthroscopic pump and shaver system used during surgery.

The pressure gradient from the positive pressure of anesthesia and the ipsilateral lung is highest in the lateral decubitus position.

The other complications that can occur are subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the given instrument?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngeal mask airway

This is the image of the laryngeal mask airway (LMA).

It aids in intubation in case of difficult airway.

The laryngeal mask airway (LMA) is a supraglottic airway device that sits in the hypopharynx and partially protects the larynx from pharyngeal secretions, but not gastric regurgitation.

Position:

* Distal tip lies against the Upper esophageal sphincter.

* Proximal tip juxtaposed with base of the tongue.

* Side cuffs cover pyriform fossa.

Contraindications:

* Parapharyngeal abscess

* Pharyngeal obstruction

* Restrictive airway disease

* Hiatal hernia

* Pregnancy

Option a:

Guedel airway -

It is an oral airway which is used to create and maintain air passage between tongue and posterior pharyngeal wall.

Option c:

Endotracheal tube -

Endotracheal intubation is usually performed emergency procedure to secure airway where endotracheal tube is placed in the trachea by passing it through mouth or nose.

Option d:

Nasogastric tube –

It is passed into the stomach via nose. It has many diagnostic and therapeutic uses like aspiration of stomach contents, evaluation of upper GI bleed, stomach wash in case of poisoning etc.

Pearl PF1542: Indications and contraindications of Laryngeal mask airway (LMA)

Indication:

* Difficult airway management during cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

* In emergency where intubation & mask ventilation is not possible.

* For minor surgeries, where Anesthetist wants to avoid intubation.

* As a conduit for bronchoscopes, small size tubes, gum elastic bougies.

* Mouth opening < 1.5cm

Contraindications:

* Oropharyngeal abscess or mass

* Conditions with high risk of aspiration:

* Hiatus hernia

* Pregnancy

* Full stomach patients who are vulnerable to go in bronchospasm

* Low pulmonary compliance (eg. Obesity)

* Peak inspiratory pressure > 20 cm of H2O.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient who has a fibroma and is deemed as a moderate to severe cardiac disease patient, which of the following surgeries are contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparascopic hysterectomy

In moderate to severe cardiac disease, laparoscopic surgery is avoided which in the above options is laparoscopic hysterectomy.

Laparoscopic procedures involve creating a pneumoperitoneum which can lead to decompensation of heart function.

Risk stratification of cardiac patients for noncardiac surgery is :

High (>5%)
Vascular procedures like aortic and other peripheral vascular surgery

Intermediate (1% to 5%)
Intraperitoneal and intrathoracic, carotid endarterectomy, head and neck surgery, orthopedic surgery, prostate surgeries.

Low(<1 %)
Endoscopic, superficial, cataract, breast, and ambulatory surgeries

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuohy needle

This is the image of a Tuohy needle that is used to provide epidural anesthesia. It can be recognized by its curved (Huber) tip and the markings made at 1 cm intervals along its length.

Other options:

Options A and B: The image below shows spinal needles are long thin needles that are classified based on their tip into:

* Cutting needles: Quincke-Babcock, Pitkin

* Pencil tip needles: Whitacre and Sprotte

Option D: The instrument below is the Quincke Needle used in spinal anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is this device called?
options: Endotracheal tubes equipped with bronchial blockers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Double-lumen endotracheal tube

The image given shows Double-lumen endotracheal tubes –to facilitate lung isolation and one-lung ventilation.

Other endotracheal tubes:

Option A: Armored or reinforced tubes: They are flexible, spiral wound tubes which are reinforced with an embedded coil so as to minimize kinking. They are useful in head and neck surgeries and when the patient is in prone position.

Option C: Ring-adair-elwin type of endotracheal tube.It is preferable for nasal and ophthalmic surgeries because it has a preformed right-angle bend at the level of the teeth so that it doesn’t disrupt the surgical field.

Option D: Endotracheal tubes equipped with bronchial blockers – which can also facilitate lung isolation and one-lung ventilation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is contraindicated in patients with acute intermittent porphyria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thiopentone

Thiopentone cannot be administered in a patient with acute intermittent porphyria.

Thiopentone is a barbiturate induces aminolevulinic acid synthetase, which increases the formation of porphyrins. This will precipitate porphyria attacks, especially acute intermittent porphyria or variegate porphyria in susceptible individuals.

Other effects:

Thiopentone

* is cerebroprotective as it reduces CSF volume by facilitating its absorption.

* also decreases cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume and helps in lowering intracranial pressure.

* should be avoided in hypovolemic or shock patients because of the significant reduction in cardiac output (69%) and arterial blood pressure due to vasodilation and venous pooling.

* produces dose-related central respiratory depression, producing a characteristic ventilatory pattern called 'double apnea'.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 14G

In this case, since large volume replacement is needed and is hypotensive, a 14 gauge cannula has to be used which delivers fluids at a rate of 270 ml/min.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During recovery from anesthesia, a patient started experiencing hallucinations and vivid dreams. Which inducing agent is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ketamine

Hallucinations and vivid dreams during recovery from anesthesia are a manifestation of an emergence reaction following the administration of ketamine.

The incidence of psychic emergence reactions ranges from 3% to 100% and is usually associated with excitement, confusion, euphoria, and fear. The symptoms usually appear in the first hour of emergence and subside within several hours.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Intravenous induction agent of choice for day care anesthesia is____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Propofol

Intravenous induction agent of choice for day care anesthesia is propofol.

* It has rapid onset of action and a faster recovery.

* It also reduces postoperative nausea and vomiting which provide yet another reason for it to be a preferred drug for outpatient anesthesia.

Note -

* Inhalational agent of choice for day care anesthesia is sevoflurane.

* Muscle relaxant of choice for day care anesthesia is rocuronium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Block sodium channels

Local anesthetics primarily act by blocking the sodium channels bound to the membrane.

Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states :

* Resting (non conducting)

* Open (conducting) and

* Inactivated (non conducting)

The local anesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium.

Local anesthetics have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in open and inactivated state than in the resting state.

Local anesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibers are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations.

Note:

Local anesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors. But blocking of sodium channels is the best answer, of all the given options.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is the anaesthesia of choice in a day care dental surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infiltration anesthesia

Infiltration anesthesia is ideal to perform in day care dental procedures as a fast-track procedure.

It has a lesser incidence of complications than regional or general anesthesia. Other anesthetic techniques for hernia repair include intercostal block and ilioinguinal nerve block.

Ambulatory/Outpatient anesthesia employs the use of fast - Track surgical techniques to provide adequate surgical anesthesia and minimize post-operative complications in order to reduce the duration of hospital stay.

Disadvantage of infiltration anesthesia - Short duration of anesthesia even when long-acting local anesthetics like bupivacaine are used. Extended- duration local anesthesia can be produced by encapsulating bupivacaine into a biodegradable carrier.

Regional anesthesia is contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders, those on anticoagulants and with local infections.

Spinal anesthesia has the disadvantage over epidural anesthesia of delayed recovery due to profound motor blockade. Spinal opioids like fentanyl or sufentanil are added to prolong postoperative analgesia and minimize motor block without delaying recovery. But the adverse effects of spinal opioids like nausea, pruritus and postoperative urinary retention are additive.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The mask given below works on which of the following principles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bernoulli principle

The given image shows a Venturi mask and it works using the Bernoulli principle in delivering a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient.

In the Venturi mask ,the size of the constriction present in the device determines the final concentration of oxygen for a given gas flow. This is achieved in spite of the patient's respiratory pattern by providing a higher gas flow than the peak inspiratory flow rate.

Patients with COPD require greater FiO2 than those provided by low-flow devices and are ideal candidates for the use of a Venturi mask.

In the Venturi mask system, oxygen inflow is connected to a specific color-coded entrainment device at the base of the mask that provides a set Fio2 at a set oxygen inflow rate. Various entrainment devices can provide a Fio2 of 0.24 to 0.5, with an oxygen inflow of 4 to 15 l/min and a delivered total flow of 35 to 45 l/min.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following induction agents is most appropriate for a patient with cardiac disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate is considered to be the most appropriate induction agent for cardiac patients.

Etomidate has minimal effect on cardiovascular function due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptors. They act on alpha 2 adrenoreceptors and increase blood pressure which helps to maintain cardiovascular stability after the induction.

Etomidate is the induction agent of choice in patients with cardiovascular disease, reactive airway disease, and intracranial hypertension,

Due to its unique hemodynamic stability, it is used as a short-term sedative in hemodynamically unstable patients like patients requiring cardioversion or in patients with unstable angina for minor operative procedures.

Long-term use of etomidate in trauma or terminally ill patients will cause a reversible inhibition on 11 beta-hydroxylase which decreases cortisol production and increase 11 deoxycorticosterone. This results in adrenocortical suppression.

Other options:

Option A- Ketamine has a stimulatory effect on the sympathetic nervous system and results in increased blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This leads to an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption and so it is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease.

Option C- Propofol is a myocardial depressant agent. It reduces sympathetic activity, leading to vasodilatation that results in a reduction of blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

Option D- Thiopentone is also a myocardial depressant agent. It causes peripheral vasodilatation, reduction in the ventricular filling, negative inotropic effect, and reduction in a sympathetic outflow from CNS. this results in a reduction in blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While doing a subclavian venous catheterization, the patient suddenly desaturated and on examination of the chest, there was hyper resonance in the apical area of the right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumothorax

A common complication of subclavian vein catheterization is pneumothorax and it is the diagnosis in this case as there is hyper resonance and sudden desaturation.

However, the most common complication of a central line insertion is an arterial puncture.

Complications of central vein catheterization are

* Arterial puncture- this is the most common complication.

* Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of puncture of intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.

* Pneumothorax- injury to the underlying pleura may lead to pneumothorax. This is more common in subclavian vein catheterization.

* Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterization. But it is not the most common.

* Injury to the associated nerves like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.

* Thromboembolism leading to venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism is more common with femoral veins.

* Infections

Central venous catheterization is the insertion of the catheter into a large central vein. The veins preferred largely depend on the underlying disease in the patient, the clinical setting, and the expertise of the doctor.

The internal jugular vein is preferred when the patient has:

* Bleeding diathesis- Bleeding from this vein can be easily detected and can be controlled with pressure.

* Pneumothorax- The lesser risk of injury to the lung

* Needs cardiac pacing- right internal jugular vein is used.

Femoral or subclavian veins can be used in patients when the neck is immobilized using a cervical collar.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An ICU patient who was already on endotracheal intubation now requires a tracheostomy. Which type of tube will you use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cuffed tracheostomy tube

A cuffed tracheostomy tube is used in this patient for tracheostomy.

Cuffed tracheostomy is preferred in unconscious patients or patients on ventilators for a long time. When the cuff is inflated, it not only prevents the aspiration of pharyngeal secretions into the trachea but also prevents the leakage of air. The cuff should be deflated every 2 hours for 5 minutes to prevent pressure necrosis of the cartilage and trachea.

Metallic tubes(Option C) and uncuffed tracheostomy(Option A) tubes are not used too commonly because of the risk of displacement and aspiration of secretions into the trachea.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Resistance to the airflow through the tube shown below is primarily because of :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diameter

The airway device shown in the image is an endotracheal tube and the resistance to the airflow through it primarily depends on diameter(Internal diameter).

* The size of an endotracheal tube usually refers to the internal diameter in mm. Rarely the French scale is used where the size corresponds to the external diameter multiplied by 3.

* For adults, usually, a 7-mm is used for women and a 7.5 or 8-mm ETT is used for men.

* Generally, high-volume, low-pressure cuffed tubes are used in adults, and cuffless tubes are used in neonates and infants.

* Besides age, the choice of an endotracheal tube also depends on the presence of airway pathologies and the reason behind the placement of the tube.

* Smaller-sized tubes lead to increase airway resistance and increased work breathing.

* Larger tubes have a higher risk of laryngeal and tracheal trauma and sore throat.

Correct answer: C. Venturi mask

Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min. It is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation. It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2.

It is usually limited to a flow of 5-6 L/min to reduce the discomfort resulting from inadequate humidification and high flow into the nasal cavity. Option B: Hudson mask also known as a simple face mask is a Low-flow, variable-performance device. It provides an oxygen flow rate of up to 5-10 L/min and provides a variable FiO2. This type of mask is used in patients with significant hypoxia, with relatively normal ventilation, such as victims of trauma or carbon monoxide exposure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhalational agent of choice in a 10-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sevoflurane

Induction agent of choice in pediatric anesthesia is sevoflurane.

Although both halothane and sevoflurane provide a smooth induction, sevoflurane appears to have a greater therapeutic index than halothane and is the preferred agent for inhaled induction in pediatric anesthesia.

Isoflurane and desflurane are airway irritants. Hence not used for induction of anesthesia as they can precipitate laryngospasm. These agents are used only during maintenance of anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is most suitable for intravenous regional anesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lidocaine

Lidocaine is the most preferred drug for intravenous regional anesthesia.

Intravenous Regional Anesthesia or Bier’s block:

* Intravenous administration of LA into a tourniquet-occluded limb.

* Anesthesia for short surgical procedures (<45-60 minutes) on the limbs(such as the excision of soft tissue masses or carpal tunnel release)

* LA commonly used are Lidocaine (most common), followed by Prilocaine, Mepivacaine, Chloroprocaine, Procaine, and Etidocaine.

* For upper limbs, 40 mL of 0.5% lidocaine without epinephrine is used.

* For lower limbs, 50 to 100 mL of 0.25% lidocaine without epinephrine is used.

Complications following Bier's block are postoperative pain, difficulty in providing bloodless field, and in rare cases may lead to compartment syndrome due to increased pressure applied. Premature deflation of the tourniquet or increased dose of local anesthesia may lead to systemic toxicity.

Bupivacaine (Option A) is no longer used for Biers block. This is because Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic (LA). Accidental early deflation of the tourniquet can lead to massive systemic doses of bupivacaine resulting in cardiac arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is brought in to the casualty with maxillofacial trauma after an RTA. He is unconscious with a dropping SpO2. The ER doctor decides to intubate him. What is the preferred method of intubation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheostomy

Patients with severe maxillofacial trauma are very likely to experience severe airway compromise or obstruction. Hence to maintain airway competency, intubation is necessary and in the above case, the presence of facial trauma, tracheostomy is ideal.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

* Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.

* Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance

* Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood

* Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.

* Allows positive pressure respiration

* Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

* Respiratory obstruction due to

* Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures

* Neoplasms

* Foreign bodies or edema

* Bilateral abductor paralysis

* Congenital anomalies

* Retained secretions

* Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions

* Painful cough

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Other options:

Option A and B: Mask ventilation and LMA are not enough as the patient has severe airway compromise.

Option D:  In cases of facial trauma, nasotracheal intubation is avoided due to the risk of the tube entering the brain through an undiagnosed basal skull fracture.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young male patient was given regional block with 0.25% bupivacaine for a minor surgical procedure. Shortly after the injection, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and the pulse was not recordable. Which of the following would be the best course of management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CPR with 20% intralipid

The clinical picture of an unresponsive patient with an absent pulse following bupivacaine administration is most likely due to bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity resulting from accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic. The best course of management in this scenario would be administering CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), along with a 20% intralipid injection.

Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic that is the most cardiotoxic among the local anesthetics. It depresses the rapid phase of depolarization in Purkinje fibers and ventricular muscle due to a decreased availability of fast sodium channels in cardiac membranes. This reduced rate of depolarization depresses myocardial contractility. Hence, bupivacaine is a potent cardio depressant.

Cardio-vascular effects of bupivacaine-induced toxicity are as follows:

* Left ventricular depression

* Atrioventricular heart block

* Ventricular arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation

* Sinus bradycardia can lead to cardiac arrest

Initial management includes immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation as per the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) algorithm.

Following CPR, intralipid therapy is initiated. Its mechanism is explained by the lipid sink theory which states lipophilic drugs (bupivacaine) are absorbed into the lipid emulsion of the plasma, hence, removed from tissues affected by toxicity. Intralipid therapy is administered as :

* 20% IV dose as a rapid bolus (1.5 mL/kg)

* Infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min for 10 min after the patient is hemodynamically stable

Local anesthesia systemic toxicity (LAST) can also affect the central nervous system (CNS), which is more susceptible to local anesthetic action as compared to the cardiovascular system. Dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation are the initial symptoms. Shivering, muscular twitching, and tremors follow. Tonic-clonic seizures occur. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest.

Pearl PF2259: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

The adult cardiac arrest algorithm is based on the AHA guidelines as shown below.

Pearl PF1780: High quality CPR for adults

* Push hard: 5-6cm depth

* Push fast: 100-120/min frequency

* Allow for complete chest recoil

* Minimize interruptions in compressions <10 seconds

* Avoid excessive ventilation

* Rotate compressor every 2 min or earlier if fatigued

* If no advanced airway, 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio

Attempt to improve CPR quality if :

* Quantitative waveform capnography - PETCO2 <10mmHg,

* Intra-arterial pressure - If relaxation phase (diastolic) pressure <20mmHg

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: BIPAP cannot be considered in patients with which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Unconscious patients

Patients being unconscious in considered a contraindication for BiPAP.

BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) therapy is a non-invasive ventilation technique that requires patient cooperation and the ability to breathe spontaneously. It relies on the patient's ability to initiate and maintain breathing efforts while receiving pressure support from the device. An unconscious patient, by definition, lacks the ability to consciously control their breathing and cannot actively participate in the breathing process. Therefore, BiPAP therapy is contraindicated in unconscious patients as they cannot tolerate the interface and settings required for this type of ventilation.

In such cases, invasive mechanical ventilation, which provides full ventilatory support, is typically necessary to maintain adequate gas exchange and support respiratory function.

Positive-pressure ventilation helps with stiff lungs and high airway resistance. Here, gas flow and pressure can be adjusted to improve inflation. Disadvantages include poor ventilation-perfusion matching, lower cardiac output, and lung injury. Increased chest pressure reduces blood return to the heart. Barotrauma results from high pressures, and volutrauma occurs from repeated alveolar collapse and reopening. Air flows to the upper lung areas, while blood flows to the lower regions, increasing the dead space.

Other Options:

Option (a) Low pO2 levels: BiPAP therapy is often utilized to improve oxygenation in patients with hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels). By delivering positive airway pressure, BiPAP helps to recruit collapsed alveoli, improve lung ventilation-perfusion matching, and enhance oxygen diffusion into the bloodstream. Therefore, low pO2 levels are not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; instead, they may indicate the need for BiPAP to support oxygenation.

Option (c) High CO2 levels: BiPAP therapy can also be beneficial for patients with hypercapnia (elevated blood carbon dioxide levels), such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation or obesity hypoventilation syndrome. By providing inspiratory pressure support and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), BiPAP assists ventilation, enhances alveolar ventilation, and helps to eliminate excess carbon dioxide from the body. Therefore, high CO2 levels alone do not contraindicate the use of BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP may be indicated to improve ventilation and reduce CO2 levels.

Option (d) Obstructive sleep apnea: BiPAP therapy is commonly employed as a non-invasive treatment for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a sleep disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway collapse during sleep. By delivering two levels of pressure – higher pressure during inspiration (IPAP) and lower pressure during expiration (EPAP) – BiPAP helps to keep the upper airway open, prevent apnea events, and improve sleep quality. Therefore, obstructive sleep apnea is not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP is a recommended treatment modality for managing this condition.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Epidural anesthesia involves local anesthetic administration between
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dura and ligamentum flavum

Epidural anesthesia involves local anesthetic administration between the dura and ligamentum flavum.

Subdural injection (seen in a failed spinal anesthesia) is between dura and arachnoid.

Spinal anesthesia (subarachnoid block, intrathecal block) involves local anesthetic administration between the pia and arachnoid mater.

In spinal anesthesia, the local anesthetic is injected into CSF, which bathes the nerve root. Hence, a relatively small dose and volume of local anesthetic is sufficient to achieve dense sensory and motor blockade.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The first step in the management of a hemodynamically stable patient with the following rhythm is_____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravenous Amiodarone

Intravenous Amiodarone is the first step in the management of a hemodynamically stable patient with a rhythm strip showing ventricular tachycardia. The above EKG shows rapid heart rate (>100 bpm), regular rhythm, wide complex QRS (>120 ms), all QRS complexes are similar (monomorphic). This EKG diagnostic of a sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT).

Intravenous amiodarone is recommended by the AHA/ACC 2015 guidelines for the treatment of hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia.

Chest compressions are the first step in unresponsive patients without a pulse.

Synchronized cardioversion is the treatment of choice for hemodynamically unstable patients (hypotension, respiratory distress, altered sensorium) with ventricular tachycardia.

Carotid massage is contraindicated in ventricular tachycardia.

Note: IV Lidocaine / IV Procainamide can also be used if amiodarone is unavailable in the above scenario depicted in the question.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following inhalational agents has the blood-gas partition coefficient similar to Nitrous oxide?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Desflurane

Desflurane is the inhalational anesthetic agent with the blood-gas partition coefficient similar to Nitrous oxide.

Among the commonly used inhalational anesthetics, desflurane is the least fat-soluble which leads to a faster recovery. Desflurane is also minimally metabolized by the liver, thereby reducing hepatotoxicity.

Inhalational agent
Blood-gas partition coefficient

Halothane
2.5

Isoflurane
1.4

Sevoflurane
0.65

Desflurane
0.45

Nitrous oxide
0.4

Blood-gas partition co-efficient determines the solubility of the anesthetic agent in the blood. The higher the blood-gas partition coefficient, the higher will be the solubility of the anesthetic agent. This leads to its greater uptake by pulmonary circulation. The higher the uptake of the anesthetic agent, the higher the difference between the inspired and alveolar concentrations, which leads to a slower rate of induction and recovery. Desflurane has a very low blood:gas partition coefficient (0.42). Thus, the alveolar and blood concentrations rapidly rise to the level of inspired concentration, providing rapid induction of anesthesia and rapid recovery.

Other options:

Option A- Halothane is a high fat-soluble agent and can result in halothane hepatitis due to increased metabolism in obese individuals. Hence it is avoided.

Option C- Sevoflurane has a relatively higher fat solubility compared to desflurane.

Option D- Isoflurane has a higher fat-gas partition co-efficient resulting in increased recovery time from anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery in 5 days is taking aspirin, a multivitamin, enalapril, and metoprolol. What is the appropriate perioperative management for this patient?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop enalapril

In the given clinical scenario, where a patient is scheduled for elective hip surgery in 5 days and is taking aspirin, a multivitamin, enalapril, and metoprolol, the recommended perioperative management includes discontinuing enalapril, as it is an ACE inhibitor.

ACE inhibitors are discontinued 24 hours before surgery due to the risk of hemodynamic instability. ACE inhibitors block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to vasodilation and reduced blood pressure. During anaesthesia, there is already vasodilation and decreased sympathetic tone → combining this with ACE inhibitors can cause severe hypotension that is resistant to fluids.
Aspirin can be maintained unless the patient is scheduled for neurosurgery or retinal surgery, provided the dosage remains unchanged. Metoprolol, being a beta-blocker, should always be continued.

Pearl PF1221: Drugs that should be discontinued prior to surgery

Drugs that should be discontinued prior to surgery

* Topical medications - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Diuretics except thiazides - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Oral hypoglycemic agents - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Sildenafil - Discontinue 24 hours before the day of surgery

* NSAIDs - Discontinue 48 hours before the day of surgery

* Warfarin - Discontinue 4 days before surgery, except for patients having cataract surgery without a bulbar block.

* Short-acting Insulins except when given by a continuous pump

* Thienopyridines (e.g., clopidogrel, ticlopidine) except in cataract surgery, patients with metallic/drug-eluting stents

* Aspirin should be discontinued 3 days before the surgery, in selected cases where reversal of platelet inhibition is necessary

* MAO Inhibitors - 2 weeks prior (MAO Inhibitors are usually continued.They should be discontinued if the patient and anesthesiologist factors are not favourable to continue them)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery receives succinylcholine for muscle relaxation and later develops hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene.

Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscles and inhibits calcium-induced calcium release. This results in the uncoupling of membrane depolarisation and muscle contraction, thus inhibiting muscle contraction.

Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic condition in which mutated RyR1 receptors are present in the skeletal muscles. In the presence of certain triggers, this mutated RyR1 causes severe dysfunction in the RyR1 channels. This leads to the accumulation of calcium ions in the skeletal muscle, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, rigidity, increased heat production, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, and increased end-tidal CO₂.

Drugs triggering malignant hyperthermia:

* Succinylcholine

* Halothane

* Isoflurane

* Sevoflurane

Susceptible patients:

* Patients with a positive family history. It can be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

* Patients with congenital myopathies.

Treatment:

Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia. Once the diagnosis is made, the causative inhalational agent should be stopped immediately. Supportive treatment with rapid cooling, inhalation of 100% oxygen, control of acidosis, and treatment of hyperkalaemia should be given.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the most likely cause when a patient under general anaesthesia develops left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side during auscultation? PPV-Positive pressure ventillation
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right endobronchial intubation

The most likely cause of left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side, is endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

Endobronchial intubation is first indicated by a sudden rise in peak inspiratory pressure.
Capnography and detection of end-tidal CO2 is the confirmation for an advanced airway placement, but it does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation.

Signs of endobronchial intubation:

* Elevated peak inspiratory pressure (first sign)

* Asymmetric chest expansion

* Unilateral breath sounds

* Drop in oxygen saturation (hypoxemia)

Other options:

Option A: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube- will lead to diminished breath on both sides.

Option B: Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV- less likely to occur immediately after intubation. It may be seen after prolonged PPV, post-intubation. It is a serious complication of mechanical ventilation. It is rare in intubated patients with normal lungs and most patients with pneumothorax related to mechanical ventilation (PRMV) have underlying lung diseases that range from primary obstructive lung disease to secondary pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Excessive airway pressure during mechanical ventilation can rupture alveoli, leading to air leakage into the pleural space → pneumothorax.

Option C: Intraoperative bronchospasm is usually manifested as wheezing, increasing peak airway pressure, and a slowly rising waveform on the capnograph.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the newly added sixth link in the chain of survival according to the latest AHA update? AHA-American Health Association
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recovery and Rehabilitation

The newly added sixth link in the chain of survival according to the latest AHA update is Recovery and Rehabilitation.

The AHA (American Heart Association) Chain of Survival is a critical concept in improving survival rates for individuals experiencing cardiac arrest. It consists of a series of actions that, when performed promptly and effectively, increase the chances of survival. Traditionally, the chain includes five key links: early recognition and activation of emergency response, early CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, and post-cardiac arrest care. Each of these steps plays a vital role in ensuring timely intervention, restoring circulation, and providing critical care to improve patient outcomes.

In recent updates, the AHA has introduced a sixth link to the Chain of Survival: Recovery. This emphasizes the importance of long-term rehabilitation, psychological support, and follow-up care for cardiac arrest survivors. Recovery includes interventions such as physical therapy, lifestyle modifications, and emotional support to help survivors regain quality of life and reduce the risk of future cardiac events. This addition highlights the growing recognition that survival is not just about resuscitation but also about ensuring a patient's overall well-being beyond the immediate crisis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not reversed with the administration of glycopyrolate?
options: Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade

Glycopyrrolate can reverse all conditions except muscle weakness caused by neuromuscular blockade.

Anticholinergic drugs like glycopyrrolate and atropine are not used to reverse neuromuscular blockade. They only attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents.

Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:

* Cholinesterase inhibitors - Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine.

* Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.

* L-cysteine causes the inactivation of gantacurium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing an open laparotomy. Which among the following is best as a maintenance infusion during surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crystalloid

The IV fluid of choice in the intraoperative period is crystalloid.

The rationale is that these effectively increase the plasma volume more than other fluids. Although colloids have similar effects, the potential toxicities of colloids have replaced colloids by crystalloids in most setups.

In cases of high risk cases, it is advisable to monitor the cardiac output with invasive methods for early detection of hypovolumea and hypotension. in such cases, fluid volume has to be titrated.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which among the following is not a component used in ACLS?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium bicarbonate

Sodium bicarbonate injection is not a part of ACLS guidelines.

The drugs used in ACLS are:

* Epinephrine/ Adrenaline

* Amiodarone

* Lignocaine

* Beta-blockers

Magnesum sulphate may sometimes be included as it can be used in Torsades de pointes and hypomagnesemia

Defibrillator is also a part of ACLS.

Pearl PF1767: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which anaesthetic scoring system is shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mallampatti classification

The image shows grading system to assess difficulty of laryngeal intubation called Mallampatti classification

It consists of 4 classes.

Other options

1. The Cormack and Lehane grading scale describes laryngoscopic views with grades ranging from I (the best view) to IV (the most difficult view). The grades are as follows :

2. ASA physical status classification is to assess the relative risk of sedation and surgical anesthesia. it has grades from I to VI with I being healthy individual and VI being brain brain-dead patient.

3. Brodsky classification is the grading of palatine tonsil hypertrophy

Pearl PF0609: Predictors of Difficult Airway

Risk factors:

* Obstructive sleep apnea

* History of snoring

* Obesity

* Facial and neck deformities from previous surgery

* Previous head and neck radiation

* Head and neck trauma

* Congenital abnormalities of the head and neck

* Rheumatoid arthritis

* Down syndrome

* Scleroderma

* Cervical spine disease or previous cervical spine surgery

Specific tests for assessment:

* Mallampati scores (III and IV)

* Thyromental distance <6.5 cm with head in maximum extension

* Sterno-mental distance <12.5 cm with head in maximum extension

* Increased neck circumference (>17 inches in men or >16 inches in women)

* Upper lip bite test : Inability to protrude the mandible or lower teeth in front of the upper teeth

* Cormack and Lehane (laryngoscopic view) - Grade III and IV

Although the presence of these risk factors may not be sensitive in detecting a difficult intubation, the absence of these findings indicates an ease with intubation.

Pearl PF1743: Samsoon & Young's Modified Mallampati Classification

Samsoon & Young's Modified Mallampati Classification is used to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation.

* Class I: soft palate, fauces, entire uvula, pillars;

* Class II: soft palate, fauces, the portion of uvula;

* Class III: soft palate, the base of uvula;

* Class IV: hard palate only.

Initially, the Mallampatti scoring system (1985) had only 3 classes. This was modified by Samsoon and Young to include class 4. Later class 0 was also added.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following undergoes Hofmann elimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atracurium

Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation.

Rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion. Pancuronium excretion is primarily renal. A small percentage of the drug is excreted through bile (hepatic elimination).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing elbow surgery was given a local anaesthetic during the procedure. Local anaesthetics acts by ___________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blocking voltage gated sodium channels

Local anaesthetics primarily act by blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels bound to the membrane.

Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states :

* Resting (non-conducting)

* Open (conducting)

* Inactivated (non-conducting)

The local anaesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium. They have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in the open and inactivated state than in the resting state.

Local anaesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibres are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations.

Note:

Local anaesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors, but blocking sodium channels is its primary action.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: According to the American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) classification, what grade is given to a normal healthy individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ASA I

A normal healthy individual is given ASA I grade.

Pearl PF1220: American Society of Anesthesiologists’ Physical Status Classification of Patients

American Society of Anesthesiologists’(ASA) classification is used to define relative risk prior to conscious sedation and surgical anesthesia.

It is simple, reproducible and strongly correlates to perioperative risk.

ASA PS Classification & Definition
Examples, including, but not limited to:

ASA I: A normal healthy patient
Healthy, non-smoking, no or minimal alcohol use

ASA II: A patient with mild systemic disease
Without substantive functional limitations. Eg: current smoker, social alcohol drinker, pregnancy, obesity (30 < BMI < 40), well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease

ASA III: A patient with severe systemic disease
Substantive functional limitations; One or more moderate to severe diseases. Eg: poorly controlled DM or HTN, COPD, morbid obesity (BMI ≥40), active hepatitis, alcohol dependence or abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction of ejection fraction, ESRD undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis, premature infant PCA < 60 weeks, history (>3 months) of MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents.

ASA IV: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life
Eg: recent ( < 3 months) MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents, ongoing cardiac ischemia or severe valve dysfunction, severe reduction of ejection fraction, sepsis, DIC, ARD or ESRD not undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis

ASA V: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation
Eg: ruptured abdominal/thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischemic bowel in the face of significant cardiac pathology or multiple organ/system dysfunction

ASA VI: A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During recovery from anaesthesia, which of the following drugs is used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neostigmine

Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor commonly used during reversal of anaesthesia.

Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:

Cholinesterase inhibitors - Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine.
Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.
L-cysteine causes the inactivation of gantacurium.

Other options:

Option B, C:  Anticholinergic drugs like glycopyrrolate and atropine are not used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade. They only attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents.

Option D: Propofol is a barbiturate group of drug which is used for induction of anaesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Malampatti classification is used to:
options: Anticipate a difficult airway for endotracheal intubation
Evaluate a patient for orogastric intubation
Evaluate the risk of blood loss during surgery
Evaluate the cardiovascular fitness of the patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anticipate a difficult airway for endotracheal intubation

The modified Mallampatti classification is used in the assessment of airway. It is a predictor of the difficulty of intubation or difficult airway.

The assessment is performed with the patient sitting up straight, mouth open and tongue maximally protruded, without saying "ahh."

Modified Mallampati classification:

* Class 0: Ability to see any part of the epiglottis.

* Class I: Soft palate, fauces, uvula visible.

* Class II: Soft palate and fauces seen, tip of uvula not visible.

* Class III: Soft palate, base of uvula visible.

* Class IV: Soft palate not visible at all. Only hard palate visible.

Classes 3 and 4 are difficult intubation situations.

*Note:
Initially, the Mallampatti scoring system (1985) had only 3 classes. This was modified by Samsoon and Young to include class 4. Later class 0 was also added.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths is given during CPR in an adult if 2 rescuers are present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30:2

During cardiopulmonary resuscitation of adults, the ratio of chest compression to rescue breaths is 30:2 irrespective of the number of rescuers.

In infants and children, the ratio is 30:2 for a single rescuer and 15:2 if 2 or more rescuers are present.

Pearl PF1780: High quality CPR for adults

* Push hard: 5-6cm depth

* Push fast: 100-120/min frequency

* Allow for complete chest recoil

* Minimize interruptions in compressions <10 seconds

* Avoid excessive ventilation

* Rotate compressor every 2 min or earlier if fatigued

* If no advanced airway, 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio

Attempt to improve CPR quality if :

* Quantitative waveform capnography - PETCO2 <10mmHg,

* Intra-arterial pressure - If relaxation phase (diastolic) pressure <20mmHg

Pearl PF2036: Basic Life Support (BLS) Algorithm

Pearl PF1767: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following anaesthetic agents act on NMDA receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ketamine

Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that inhibits NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors resulting in a decrease in excitatory stimulation by glutamate in the brain. It is a strong analgesic and amnestic agent.

On the cardiovascular system, it directly has a cardio-depressive effect and indirectly stimulates it by activating the sympathetic system and inhibiting the vagus nerve. It predominantly shows a stimulatory effect hence causing tachycardia, increased cardiac output, and increased systemic and pulmonary hypertension.

On the respiratory system, it has a bronchodilator effect on bronchial smooth muscles. It increases salivary secretion and bronchial secretion. It also acts on other systems and increases the intracranial and intraocular pressures.

Uses:

* Ketamine is the intravenous agent of choice for patients with shock, low cardiac output states, and reactive airway diseases.

* It is also used in patients with congenital heart diseases, especially with right-to-left shunts

* Perioperative analgesia

Ketamine should be avoided in patients with a history of seizures, psychiatric illness, or vascular aneurysms. It is also contraindicated in open-eye injuries and eye surgeries.

Adverse effects:

* Hallucination is the most common side effect of ketamine.

* Emergence reaction (vivid dreaming, illusion, etc)

* Increases brain oxygen consumption and metabolic rate leading to increased intracranial tension.

Other options:

Option A: Propofol facilitates the inhibitory neurotransmission by action on GABA-A receptors. It has a rapid onset of action (within 15 sec). Induction dose is usually 1-2 mg/ kg and the maintenance dose is 100-200 µg/ kg/ min. Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion and appears as a milky white liquid. It has antiemetic properties which help reduce post-operative nausea and vomiting.

Option C: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine that facilitates GABA-A receptors' action by increasing the frequency of opening of GABA-mediated chloride channels. It is used in treating seizures and is used in daycare surgeries as an induction agent due to its short half-life.

Option D: Thiopentone sodium belongs to the barbiturate group which acts on the GABA-A receptors. This site is separate from the GABA-A site to which benzodiazepines bind. They potentiate the action of GABA in increasing the duration of openings of chloride-specific ion channels.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 20-year-old male posted for emergency open appendicectomy was given spinal anaesthesia. On examination, cremasteric reflex was absent. What could be the possible level of spinal anaesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L2

In the given clinical scenario, the possible level of spinal anesthesia is L2 as the root value of cremasteric reflex is L1, L2.

After the administration of spinal anesthesia, monitoring of block height is done by motor, sensory, and sympathetic nervous system assessment. Spinal reflexes can also be used for monitoring the block height, which includes abdominal, cremasteric, and anal reflexes.

Cremasteric reflex is a superficial reflex that can be tested in males. The female counterpart is the Geigel reflex.

* Procedure: Stroking of the inner part of the upper thigh causes pulling up of the ipsilateral testicle

* Afferent: Ilioinguinal and femoral (sensory) branch of genitofemoral nerves (L1, L2)

* Reflex Centre: L1, L2 spinal nerve nuclei

* Efferent: Genital (motor) branch of genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) to cremasteric muscle

The level of motor blockade is 2 spinal segments lower than sensory blockade, which is in turn 2 segments lower than autonomic block. For example, if the motor block is at the level of T8, the sensory block would be at the level of T6, and the sympathetic block would be at the level of T4.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A nerve conduction study is being conducted, as shown in the image. Electrodes are positioned near the wrist, and stimulation is used to evaluate motor and sensory function. Which nerve is most likely being monitored in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulnar nerve

In the given scenario, the ulnar nerve is being monitored. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve. This assesses the contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle to monitor neuromuscular activity.

The procedure shown in the image is known as electromyography (EMG). It is the process of recording changes in muscle electric potential using surface or needle electrodes. An EMG test examines the electrical signals produced by muscles both at rest and while in use. A healthy muscle at rest does not emit any electrical signals. A damaged muscle may show electrical activity while at rest or in activity.

In order to avoid postoperative residual curarisation, an acceleromyograph can be used for neuromuscular monitoring during general anaesthesia with neuromuscular-blocking drugs.

In the image given below: (A) Placement of electrodes for physiological measurement of conduction of the ulnar nerve, based on standard surface Ag-AgCl electrodes applied differentially (21 mm centre-to-centre spacing) located along the ulnar nerve track. Centre distance: 18 cm between 5 and 4, all others 8 cm apart; (B) photo showing the location of the ulnar nerve track and the digiti minimi abductor muscle as well as the labelling of recording and triggering points.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with severe Maxillofacial trauma after a road traffic accident presented with SpO2 80% at room air. In a situation where the patient cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV), what is the next most appropriate immediate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform cricothyroidotomy

In the above clinical scenario of an RTA patient with severe maxillofacial trauma, where endotracheal intubation (Cannot Intubate, Cannot Ventilate) has failed to secure the airway, an alternate airway in the form of a surgical airway is indicated. Thus, performing a needle cricothyroidotomy is the next best step in the management of this patient.

This should be followed by percutaneous transtracheal oxygenation to provide temporary ventilation. In conditions that obstruct the airway, like edema of the glottis, laryngeal fracture, or severe oropharyngeal hemorrhage, a surgical airway is indicated.

Needle cricothyroidotomy involves inserting a needle through the cricothyroid membrane to provide short-term ventilation till a definitive airway can be achieved. A Y-connector is attached, and oxygenation is provided at 15 L/min.

Surgical cricothyroidotomy involves inserting an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube after making a transverse incision over the cricothyroid membrane. An emergency surgical airway is preferred over tracheostomy as it is easier to perform, is associated with less bleeding, and can be done quickly.

Other options:

Option A: Nasopharyngeal intubation is contraindicated in cases of severe maxillofacial trauma because of risk of basilar skull fracture (risk of injury to brain by putting the tube) and distorted anatomy making it unsafe or impossible to perform.

Option B: Supraglottic airway devices are used in difficult airway management but in case of severe macillofacial trauma, it is not preferred as it cannot bypass the distorted anatomy or complete obstruction of upper airway.

Option D: Administer Succinylcholine and Retry Intubation in a case of a patient that cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV) is very dangerous and ineffective as repeating might do more harm by increasing airway trauma, edema and worsened oxygenation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a day care setting, a patient is scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia. Which of the following factors makes him unfit for day care surgery?
options: His home is a 45 minute drive from the hospital
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively

A patient who does not have any provision for postoperative care is unfit for a day care surgery.

Physical fitness for the procedure, short duration, and a home environment that can support recovery and postoperative care are all important factors when choosing daycare surgery for a patient.

When selecting a patient, it is important to consider the following:

* Medically, the physiological health of the patient is of greater importance than their chronological age. For short procedures, the current health status will help us decide if the patient will tolerate the procedure or not. Chronological age becomes more important for longer, more invasive surgeries.

* Surgically, the procedure should ideally last less than 2 hours, and the patient should be able to consume liquids and possibly some solid food by the time they get discharged on the same day.

* Socially, it is important to identify a designated caregiver for the patient, at least for the first 24 hours after surgery. Their home should also have the facilities to support their recovery, and they should be sent home with all the supplies required for their postoperative care.

Some procedures that qualify for daycare surgery are listed below:

* Arthroscopies

* Biopsy (temporal, lymph node)

* Reducing a strangulated hernia

* Incision and drainage of an abscess.

* K-wiring of a finger or wrist bone fracture

* Laparoscopic appendectomy

Patients having daycare surgery can usually be discharged when they have stable vitals, have adequately controlled pain with a prescription for further pain management at home, can perform basic activities on their own, have no evidence of incision site bleeding, have a designated caregiver, and have all the instructions required for further management at home and instructions in case of an emergency.

ASA PS (American Society of Anesthesiologists – Physical Status) classification predicts perioperative risks for a patient undergoing surgery. It has 6 classes, ranging from a normal, healthy patient to a dead/ moribund patient. Grade 3 indicates a patient with severe systemic disease (some functional limitations)

Pearl PF1220: American Society of Anesthesiologists’ Physical Status Classification of Patients

American Society of Anesthesiologists’(ASA) classification is used to define relative risk prior to conscious sedation and surgical anesthesia.

It is simple, reproducible and strongly correlates to perioperative risk.

ASA PS Classification & Definition
Examples, including, but not limited to:

ASA I: A normal healthy patient
Healthy, non-smoking, no or minimal alcohol use

ASA II: A patient with mild systemic disease
Without substantive functional limitations. Eg: current smoker, social alcohol drinker, pregnancy, obesity (30 < BMI < 40), well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease

ASA III: A patient with severe systemic disease
Substantive functional limitations; One or more moderate to severe diseases. Eg: poorly controlled DM or HTN, COPD, morbid obesity (BMI ≥40), active hepatitis, alcohol dependence or abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction of ejection fraction, ESRD undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis, premature infant PCA < 60 weeks, history (>3 months) of MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents.

ASA IV: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life
Eg: recent ( < 3 months) MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents, ongoing cardiac ischemia or severe valve dysfunction, severe reduction of ejection fraction, sepsis, DIC, ARD or ESRD not undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis

ASA V: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation
Eg: ruptured abdominal/thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischemic bowel in the face of significant cardiac pathology or multiple organ/system dysfunction

ASA VI: A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In the image shown, identify the function of the marked structure on the endotracheal tube.
options: Suctioning of lower respiratory tract secretions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prevention of aspiration

The above image of a South oral Ring-Adair-Elwyn (RAE) endotracheal tube and the arrow points toward the cuff of the endotracheal tube; the function of this cuff is to prevent aspiration.

The cuff forms a seal in the trachea, allowing delivery of high ventilation pressures and reducing the risk of aspiration. It is inflated via a pilot balloon, and cuff pressure should ideally be maintained between 20–30 cm H₂O to avoid complications.

Endotracheal tube:

Advantages:

* Considered the gold standard for securing a definitive airway.

* Protects against aspiration.

* Can be used across a range of tube sizes.

* Permits the delivery of higher ventilation pressures

Disadvantages:

* Requires more advanced skills to insert compared to supraglottic devices.

* Prolonged use may cause pressure necrosis at the cuff or oropharyngeal sites.

* Small leaks around cuff folds may allow micro-aspiration → ventilator-associated pneumonia

* Malposition risks

Other options:

Option A: Suctioning of Lower Respiratory Tract Secretions is done via the endotracheal tube (the main lumen) with a suction catheter, not via the cuff.

Option C: Monitoring Airway Pressure is achieved through a pressure monitor connected to a ventilator or a manometer; it is the function of the ventilator, not the endotracheal tube.

Option D: Facilitation of Vocal Cord Visualization is achieved during intubation via a laryngoscope; it is not a function of the endotracheal tube.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the physiological parameters does the waveform in the image represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. End-tidal carbon dioxide

A capnograph is a device that displays and records end-tidal carbon dioxide, usually as a function of time.

The normal waveform has four different phases:

Phase I: Inspiratory baseline, represents the CO2-free gas from the airways (anatomical and apparatus dead space).

Phase II: Expiratory upstroke, mixing of dead space gas with alveolar gas.

Phase III: Alveolar plateau, represents CO2-rich gas from the alveoli. The last of the alveolar gas is sampled to measure ETCO2.

Phase 0: Inspiratory downstroke and the beginning of inspiration.

Alpha angle: The transition from phase II to III.
The alpha angle can be used to assess the ventilation/perfusion of the lung. V/Q mismatches will have an alpha angle greater than 90 degrees.

Beta angle: The transition from phase III to 0.
The beta angle can be used to assess rebreathing. If rebreathing occurs, the angle is greater than 90 degrees.

questions.text: A COVID patient requires oxygen therapy.Which of the following cylinders should be used to provide oxygen for this patient?
questions.explanation:

Colour of the shoulder of oxygen cylinder in India is white, and the body is black.
