questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient undergoing cardiac surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cefazolin

First- and second-generation cephalosporins (cefazolin) are the drugs of choice for preoperative prophylaxis for cardiac surgery. Clindamycin is reserved for cases of allergy to beta-lactams and vancomycin is recommended for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is essential in reducing the risk of surgical site infections, particularly in cardiac surgery, where the consequences of infection can be severe. The choice of antibiotic depends on the patient's medical history, allergies, and the most common pathogens involved in surgical site infections for the specific surgery. In addition to cefazolin, other cephalosporins, such as cefuroxime, can also be used for prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. The timing of antibiotic administration is crucial, with the first dose typically given within 60 minutes before the incision.

Other Options:

Option A: Penicillin G is not the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is mainly used to treat infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria, such as Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and some strains of Staphylococcus aureus.

Option B: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic and is not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is typically used to treat respiratory tract infections, skin infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria.

Option C: Azithromycin, another macrolide antibiotic, is also not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is commonly used to treat respiratory tract infections, sexually transmitted infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with drowsiness and refusal to feed. On examination, the child is in a stuporous state. The ECG is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Defibrillate, check rhythm and then start CPR
Defibrillate followed by CPR for 2min, and check rhythm
Stop CPR and do cardioversion at 2 joules/ kg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Defibrillate followed by CPR for 2min, and check rhythm

The given ECG showing polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, which is a shockable rhythm, in a stuporous paediatric patient warrants immediate defibrillation followed by CPR for 2 minutes.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, especially in a paediatric patient, is often associated with severe underlying conditions and is a life-threatening rhythm disturbance. Immediate defibrillation is critical for restoring a normal rhythm.

After defibrillation, it is advisable to do CPR for 2 minutes before reassessing the rhythm for the next round of shock to ensure adequate blood circulation and oxygenation. .

Note: Cardioversion is not suitable for polymorphic VT; defibrillation is the preferred approach in such cases.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A COVID-19 patient admitted to the ICU on mechanical ventilation suddenly develops hypoxia. The patient has decreased breath sounds on the left side and increased intrathoracic pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

This patient in the above clinical scenario has developed a sudden onset of hypoxia, decreased breath sounds on one side, and increased intrathoracic pressure, along with an X-ray showing hyper lucency in the left side with tracheal and mediastinal shift to the right side is suggestive of a diagnosis of Pneumothorax.

A pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, causing lung collapse and preventing normal lung expansion, which leads to absent or diminished breath sounds over the affected area. Pneumothorax can cause a rapid increase in intrathoracic pressure, which impairs lung expansion and leads to significant hypoxia. In patients on mechanical ventilation, it delivers positive pressure to the lungs, which can exacerbate or reveal underlying pleural issues. Increased positive pressure can contribute to the development or worsening of a tension pneumothorax.

Other options:

Option B: Left-Sided Pleural Effusion: While this condition can also cause decreased breath sounds and hypoxia, it typically does not cause acute increases in intrathoracic pressure.

Option C: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): ARDS is characterized by diffuse lung inflammation and can lead to hypoxia. However, it generally does not cause localized decreased breath sounds.

Option D: Left-Sided Pneumonia: Pneumonia can cause hypoxia and decreased breath sounds but is less likely to be associated with a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing implant surgery for his upper limb. On giving general anaesthesia he develops tachycardia, sudden raise in body temperature and rigidity of muscles. What drug is most likely to have caused this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Halothane

In the clinical scenario given above, the development of tachycardia and muscle rigidity soon after administration of anesthetic agents can be due to malignant hyperthermia. Halothane is the anesthetic agent associated with this condition.

Malignant hyperthermia is a rare genetic hypermetabolic disease of the muscle. It occurs due to a mutation of the gene for the ryanodine receptor (Ryr 1), located on chromosome 19. It is an ion channel responsible for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

The symptoms develop when the patient is exposed to suxamethonium/succinylcholine or other inhaled anesthetics like halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, etc. The mutated ryanodine receptor leads to a sudden release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of the skeletal muscle. This uncontrolled increase in intracellular calcium removes the inhibition of troponin, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, and increasing adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) activity. This results in an uncontrolled hypermetabolic state with increased oxygen consumption and CO2 production, producing severe lactic acidosis and hyperthermia.

The key clinical features are:

• Succinylcholine-induced masseter muscle rigidity (causing trismus) or generalized muscle rigidity
• Tachycardia
• Hypercarbia (increased CO2 production) and reduced oxygen saturation
• Hyperthermia (rise of 1° Celsius can occur every 5 minutes)
• Arrhythmia
• Hypertension
• Myoglobinuria and myoglobinemia indicating muscle damage
• Metabolic derangements like hyperkalemia and mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis

Treatment is to discontinue the triggering agents i.e. succinylcholine followed by administration of 100% oxygen. Metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia need to be corrected. Hyperthermia must be controlled by cooling the patient. Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice. It is given at a dose of 2.5 mg/ kg intravenously and can be repeated every 5-10 minutes till the attack subsides.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient presents with stridor after prolonged intubation. The endoscopic view is shown in the image below. What is the staging system for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cotton Meyer's

This patient presenting with stridor after prolonged intubation most likely has subglottic stenosis post intubation. This condition is staged by the Cotton Meyer's grading.

Subglottic stenosis following prolonged intubation is a narrowing of the airway just below the vocal cords (subglottic region), which can lead to difficulty breathing. This condition is often a complication of endotracheal intubation due to the pressure exerted by the tube or cuff on the airway mucosa, leading to injury and scarring.

These patients present with stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness or changes in voice, and difficulty in breathing.

Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy which allows direct visualization of the subglottic area to assess the degree of stenosis.
CT or MRI may be used to evaluate the extent of narrowing and identify any underlying structural damage.

Treatment can be via endoscopic balloon or mechanical dilation, laser therapy or surgical resection may be needed to remove the stenosis in severe cases. In severe cases, a tracheostomy may be required to bypass the obstructed segment and allow for breathing.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery in the prone position is maintained on mechanical ventilation with PEEP. What is the significance of using PEEP in this scenario?
options: Prevents alveoli collapse and atelectasis of lung
Increases venous return and maintains cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevents alveoli collapse and atelectasis of lung

The significance of using positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) in the given clinical scenario is to help keep the alveoli open, preventing collapse (atelectasis), which is especially important in the prone position where certain lung regions might be more susceptible to collapse.

This is crucial in conditions where the lungs are prone to collapse, such as Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) or when the patient is in a prone position during surgery. By maintaining open alveoli, PEEP improves gas exchange, which increases oxygen levels in the blood.

Other options:

Option B: Decreases inspiratory pressure: PEEP can increase the overall inspiratory pressure by maintaining pressure in the lungs at the end of expiration.

Option C: Increases venous return and maintains cardiac output: PEEP can decrease venous return due to increased intrathoracic pressure, which may reduce cardiac output.

Option D: Reduces CO2 in alveoli: PEEP does not directly reduce CO2 in the alveoli. The effect on CO2 depends on ventilation and perfusion matching, not just PEEP alone.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An anesthetist used the airway device shown in the image given below on a patient. Which among the following statements is true regarding the adjunct?
options: It can cause damage to the teeth
It can be used in conscious patients
It can be safely used in facial trauma cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can be used in conscious patients

The image shows a nasopharyngeal airway and its insertion. The true statement is that it can be used in conscious patients.

A nasopharyngeal airway is used to provide artificial airway passage to the hypopharynx. To place a nasopharyngeal airway, the device should be lubricated and inserted into the nose with the bevel facing the nasal septum, at a 90-degree angle to the longitudinal axis of the body. It bypasses the gag reflex as they do not go through the mouth. Thus, it can be used in conscious patients or those who have been lightly anesthetized.

Care should be taken to avoid excessive force as damage to the nasal mucosa can result in epistaxis. The nasal approach should be avoided in conditions that put patients at higher risk for epistaxis. These conditions include but are not limited to coagulopathy, pregnancy, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and uncontrolled hypertension. Absolute contraindications include basilar skull fractures, facial trauma, midface disruption, and injury to the roof of the mouth.

An oropharyngeal airway is used to maintain the airway in anesthetized patients. This adjunct prevents the tongue and epiglottis from falling back against the posterior pharynx and blocking the airway. They can cause coughing, retching, or laryngospasm in conscious patients.

To place an oropharyngeal airway, the device is inserted with the curved portion facing downwards. It is then rotated 180 degrees to be put in place. The below image shows the oropharyngeal airway:

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what pressure does the marked structure open?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-40 cm H2O

In the image, the marked structure is the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve of Mapelson-C anaesthetic breathing system and it will open at the pressure of 30-40 cm H2O. This valve is designed to release gas when a certain pressure is exceeded to prevent excessive pressure from building up in the patient's airway.

The APL valve typically opens at pressures of 30-40 cm H₂O to allow for safe ventilation without causing barotrauma to the lungs. This range is appropriate for manual ventilation to prevent high airway pressures that could lead to lung injury.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Following is the image of a normal capnograph. What is true about the segment 3-4?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Alveolar gas and plateau pressure

In a capnographic waveform, the plateau phase corresponds to alveolar air and plateau pressure.

The normal waveform has four different phases:

Phase I: Inspiratory baseline, represents the CO2-free gas from the airways (anatomical and apparatus dead space).

Phase II: Expiratory upstroke, mixing of dead space gas with alveolar gas.

Phase III: Alveolar plateau, represents CO2-rich gas from the alveoli. The last of the alveolar gas is sampled to measure ETCO2.

Phase 0: Inspiratory downstroke and the beginning of inspiration.

Alpha angle: The transition from phase II to III.
The alpha angle can be used to assess the ventilation/perfusion of the lung. V/Q mismatches will have an alpha angle greater than 90 degrees.

Beta angle: The transition from phase III to 0.
The beta angle can be used to assess rebreathing. If rebreathing occurs, the angle is greater than 90 degrees.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In the following condition as shown in the radiograph, which of the following procedures would be difficult to perform? "
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheostomy

Tracheostomy would be difficult to perform in this case of pneumothorax with tracheal deviation.

The trachea is displaced from its usual midline position, making it challenging to accurately locate and access the trachea for the incision. The tracheostomy procedure requires precise placement to ensure proper airway management and avoid complications.

Steps of Tracheostomy:

• Incision: Make a vertical incision in the midline from the cricoid cartilage to above the sternal notch. For elective procedures, a 5 cm transverse incision two fingers' breadth above the sternal notch can be used for a better cosmetic outcome.
• Dissection: Dissect tissues in the midline. Displace or ligate any dilated veins encountered to control bleeding.
• Muscle Separation: Separate and retract the strap muscles of the neck laterally to expose underlying structures.
• Thyroid Isthmus Management: Displace the thyroid isthmus upwards or divide and ligate it with sutures.
• Local Anesthesia: Inject a few drops of 4% lignocaine into the trachea to suppress coughing.
• Tracheal Incision: Fix the trachea with a hook and make a vertical incision between the third and fourth tracheal rings, converting it into a circular opening. Avoid dividing the first tracheal ring to prevent perichondritis and stenosis.
• Inserting the Tube: Insert a tracheostomy tube of appropriate size into the tracheal opening and secure it with tapes.
• Avoiding Tight Suturing: Avoid tightly suturing or packing the skin incision to prevent subcutaneous emphysema.
• Dressing: Place a gauze dressing between the skin and the flange of the tracheostomy tube around the stoma to absorb secretions, provide a barrier against infection, and allow air to escape, promoting proper healing

Other Options:

Option A: Nasogastric tube insertion: Targets the esophagus, so tracheal deviation has minimal impact.

Option B: Laryngeal mask airway (LMA): Positioned over the larynx, not directly affected by tracheal deviation.

Option D: Indirect laryngoscopy: Focuses on the larynx and vocal cords, and is less influenced by the trachea’s position.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: This recovery position is appropriate for:
options: Unresponsive patient, pulse and breathing absent
Responsive patient, pulse and breathing present
Unresponsive patient, pulse and breating present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unresponsive patient, pulse and breating present

The position illustrated in the picture is known as the recovery position, and it is used in the management of patients who are unresponsive but with pulse present and breathing present.

The recovery position can help prevent complications such as aspiration and airway obstruction in unconscious individuals. Additionally, it is crucial to continuously monitor the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation while in recovery and seek immediate medical assistance. An unresponsive patient who is breathing spontaneously in the supine position is at risk of airway obstruction from their tongue, mucus, vomit, etc. A modified lateral position is used and the following 6 principles are considered while choosing which variation of recovery position to use,

1.

The victim should be in as near a true lateral position as possible, with the head dependent to allow free drainage of fluid.

2.

The position should be stable.

3.

Avoid any pressure on the chest that impairs breathing.

4.

It should be possible to turn the victim on his or her side and to return to the back easily and safely, with concern for a possible cervical spine injury.

5.

Good observation of and access to the airway should be possible.

6.

The position itself should not cause injury to the victim.

Other options:

Option A: Unresponsive with pulse and breathing absent - In this situation, the patient is in cardiac arrest and requires immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), not the recovery position. CPR involves chest compressions and rescue breaths to support circulation and respiration.

Option B: Responsive patient with pulse and breathing present- The patient should be monitored until the emergency response team arrives.

Option D: Unresponsive with pulse present and breathing absent - In this case, the patient is experiencing respiratory arrest. Rescue breathing or bag-valve-mask ventilation should be initiated to support the patient's breathing. The recovery position is not indicated in this scenario.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the procedure being done in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bier Block

The position in the image of a hand with a tourniquet occluded limb shows a Bier Block.

IVRA or Bier’s block involves the intravenous administration of a local anesthetic into a tourniquet-occluded limb. It is used to provide anesthesia for short surgical procedures (<90 minutes) on the limbs.

Other options:

Option B: The axillary nerve block provides anesthesia for short surgical procedures on the hand, wrist, or forearm.  It is performed by using a ultrasound-guided needle in the proximal axilla between the tendon of the lattisimus dorsi and the teres major.

Option C: Median nerve blocks are used for procedures involving the palmar aspect of the arm or the carpal tunnel. For a median nerve block at the elbow, the probe is placed in the elbow crease over the proximal radius and the anesthetic is injected aiming for the fascial plane between flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus.

Option D: For a wrist block, the arm is abducted with the hand in supination, following which the anesthetic is infiltrated in the dorsal aspect of the wrist. This is used for short procedures of the wrist and the fingers.

Note: Bupivacaine is not used for Biers block. It is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic. Accidental early deflation of the tourniquet can lead to massive systemic doses of bupivacaine resulting in cardiac arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is true about the following position?
options: Ideal position for bougie insertion in emergencies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sniffing position for intubation

The above image shows the sniffing position used for intubation, which is the true statement.

The sniffing position is a common head and neck alignment technique used during intubation to optimize the view of the glottis for easier insertion of the endotracheal tube. It is achieved by flexing the neck and extending the head, resembling the posture one assumes when sniffing. The position aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes to provide a straight line of sight, making the glottis more visible during direct laryngoscopy and intubation.

Steps of intubation using the sniffing position:

• Direct laryngoscopy is performed in the sniffing position, with the head elevated 5-10 cm above the surgical table, the cervical spine flexed, and the atlantooccipital joint extended.
• The epiglottis is lifted up by the tip during laryngoscopy with Miller's blade.
• While performing laryngoscopy, the scope is lifted upwards and never levered over the upper incisors.

Other options:

Option A: The sniffing position is the most commonly used position in anesthesia as it ensures patient safety by ensuring a straight line of sight, allowing for better outcomes of the procedure.

Option B: The sniffing position is not the ideal position for bougie insertion during emergencies as there is concerns for cervical spine trauma in patients in the emergency department.

Option C: The sniffing position is not the typical position for neurosurgery. Depending on the location of the surgery, different head and neck positions are used.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following agents is appropriate for reversing vecuronium when renal function tests are normal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sugammadex

Sugammadex is used for immediate reversal of vecuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade/relaxant in the given scenario.

Sugammadex is a modified γ-cyclodextrin and the first selective relaxant–binding agent based on an encapsulating principle for the inactivation of nondepolarising neuromuscular blocking drugs mainly rocuronium and vecuronium. This principle of complex formation of sugammadex and rocuronium or vecuronium in a 1:1 ratio occurs at all levels of neuromuscular blockade resulting in a more fast-acting pharmacologic reversal when compared with anticholinesterase drugs like neostigmine.

Other options:

Options A and B: Physostigmine and Rivastigmine are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which are not effective for reversing vecuronium.

Option D: Succinylcholine is a neuromuscular blocker itself and would not reverse vecuronium; it is used to induce paralysis rather than reverse it.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA)?
options: It is made of Lignocaine and ropivacaine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methohemoglobinemia is a side effect

Methemoglobinemia can develop when high doses of prilocaine are administered, typically over 600 mg.

EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetic) is a topical mixture containing prilocaine. The risk of methemoglobinemia is increased in neonates with metabolic disorders or in those receiving drugs that can impair the reduction of methemoglobin.

It is an eutectic(in fixed proportions) mixture, not necessarily equal (Option C). It consists of a 1:1 mixture of 2.5% lidocaine (Option A) and 2.5% prilocaine, not ropivacaine (Option D)

EMLA can provide adequate dermal analgesia for procedures like:

• Split skin-graft harvesting
• Venipuncture
• Intravenous cannulation in children
• Laser skin treatments
• Lithotripsy
• Circumcision

EMLA cream should not be used on mucous membranes, broken skin, infants younger than 1 month of age, or patients with a predisposition to methemoglobinemia. EMLA is applied 45-60 minutes before the procedure with an occlusive dressing. It provides analgesia up to a depth of 5 mm, which lasts for 1-2 hours.

Other side effects include- blanching of the skin, erythema, and oedema.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He is pale, diaphoretic, and hypotensive (BP 75/50 mmHg) with tachycardia. Investigations reveal a ruptured spleen with massive hemoperitoneum. He is taken for emergency exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following induction agents is the most appropriate in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ketamine

Ketamine is the induction agent of choice in patients with hypovolemic shock or trauma because it preserves airway reflexes and stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to increased heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output. Unlike most intravenous induction agents, ketamine does not cause significant cardiovascular depression, making it ideal for hemodynamically unstable patients.

Ketamine:

• Produces dissociative anesthesia
• Increases BP and HR via catecholamine release
• Maintains cardiac output
• Preserves spontaneous respiration and airway reflexes

Therefore, it is the preferred induction agent in this hemodynamically unstable patient.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sevoflurane: An inhalational anesthetic used mainly for induction in children; it causes vasodilation and hypotension, making it unsuitable in hemorrhagic shock.
• B. Propofol: Causes marked vasodilation and myocardial depression, leading to significant hypotension; contraindicated in hypovolemic shock.
• C. Thiopentone sodium: Produces myocardial depression and peripheral vasodilation, which can worsen hypotension in trauma patients.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman is scheduled for a day-care surgical procedure for excision of a benign breast lump. Which of the following intravenous induction agents is most appropriate for this setting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Propofol

Recognize propofol as the intravenous induction agent of choice for day-care (ambulatory) surgery because of its rapid onset, short duration of action, smooth recovery, and antiemetic properties, allowing early discharge.

Why not the other options?

• A. Thiopentone: Rapid induction but slower recovery and no antiemetic effect; largely replaced by propofol for ambulatory surgery.
• C. Etomidate: Preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients due to cardiovascular stability, not for routine day-care procedures.
• D. Ketamine: Produces dissociative anesthesia with increased secretions and emergence reactions; reserved for selected indications rather than routine ambulatory anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with severe postoperative pain is given 5 mg of intravenous morphine. While monitoring him for opioid toxicity, which of the following findings would be most indicative of an opioid overdose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bradypnea

Respiratory depression (bradypnea) is the earliest and most clinically significant sign of opioid overdose. Opioids activate μ-opioid receptors in the brainstem respiratory centers, reducing the respiratory rate and the brain’s response to carbon dioxide, which can rapidly progress to respiratory failure if untreated.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tachypnea: Not a feature of opioid overdose; opioids characteristically decrease the respiratory rate.
• C. Unequal pupil (anisocoria): Suggests focal neurological disease (e.g., third nerve palsy or intracranial lesion), not opioid toxicity.
• D. Dilated pupils (mydriasis): Opioids typically cause pinpoint pupils (miosis); mydriasis may occur only in severe hypoxia or with certain opioids like meperidine.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient develops hyperthermia, g eneralized muscle rigidity, and increased end-tidal CO₂ (EtCO₂) shortly after administration of succinylcholine and sevoflurane during anaesthesia. Which of the following is the drug of choice for management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dantrolene

This presentation is classic for malignant hyperthermia, triggered by succinylcholine and volatile agents like sevoflurane. The definitive treatment is dantrolene, which inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reversing muscle rigidity, stops the hypermetabolic crisis, and rising EtCO₂.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoes cardiac surgery with muscle relaxant Vecuronium. The surgery was completed and which of the following agents is used for the reversal of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neostigmine

Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker reversed by neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. It is commonly paired with an anticholinergic agent to counter muscarinic effects.

Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

It inhibits breakdown of ACh → ↑ ACh in synaptic cleft → outcompetes vecuronium → reversal of paralysis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery develops malignant hyperthermia. Genetic testing reveals an RYR1 gene mutation. Which type of ion channel is primarily affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcium

The RYR1 gene encodes the ryanodine receptor, a calcium-release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Mutations cause uncontrolled calcium efflux, triggering the hypermetabolic crisis of malignant hyperthermia. Thus, the affected ion channel is calcium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient was undergoing surgery under general anaesthesia. For intubation, 90 mg of rocuronium was given, but the anaesthesiologist was unable to intubate the patient. What is the drug given for immediate reversal of the neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sugammadex

Sugammadex provides rapid and complete reversal of rocuronium(non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker) by encapsulating the drug molecule directly, independent of acetylcholinesterase activity. It is the preferred agent when immediate reversal is required after failed intubation with rocuronium.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: After administration of a neuromuscular blocker, a patient suddenly develops flushing of the face and becomes hypotensive. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atracurium

Atracurium is known to cause histamine release, leading to flushing, hypotension, and sometimes bronchospasm. Rocuronium, vecuronium, and cisatracurium have minimal histamine-releasing properties, making atracurium the most likely culprit in this presentation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Halothane causes a fall in blood pressure: 1. There is a 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly. 2. The early fall in blood pressure becomes parallel to the depth of anaesthesia. 3. Cardiac output decreases with deepening of anaesthesia. 4. Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Halothane produces dose-dependent cardiovascular depression, leading to a 20–30 mmHg fall in arterial blood pressure, primarily due to reduced myocardial contractility and cardiac output. Unlike many other inhalational anesthetics, halothane blunts the baroreceptor reflex, so reflex tachycardia does not occur despite hypotension.

Why is A correct?

• 1. There is a 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly: 20–30 mmHg decrease in blood pressure commonly occurs ✓
• 2. The early fall in blood pressure becomes parallel to the depth of anaesthesia: The fall in blood pressure increases with the depth of anesthesia ✓
• 3. Cardiac output decreases with deepening of anaesthesia: Cardiac output decreases as anesthesia deepens ✓
• 4. Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure: Baroreceptors are triggered due to a fall in blood pressure ✗. False – Halothane depresses the baroreceptor reflex, preventing the expected compensatory tachycardia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: IV anesthetic agent that causes adrenocortical suppression is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate inhibits 11-β-hydroxylase, blocking cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, leading to dose-dependent adrenocortical suppression. Even a single dose can reduce steroid production for 6–12 hours. Because of this, it is avoided in septic or critically ill patients who depend on adequate stress-hormone response.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The commonly used muscle relaxant with quickest onset of action and spontaneous recovery is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Suxamethonium

Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine) is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with the fastest onset and shortest duration of action among commonly used muscle relaxants. It is the drug of choice for rapid sequence induction (RSI) because it produces excellent muscle relaxation within 30–60 seconds and spontaneous recovery occurs within 5–10 minutes due to rapid hydrolysis by plasma pseudocholinesterase.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vecuronium:

• Non-depolarizing muscle relaxant
• Slower onset (2–3 minutes)
• Intermediate duration (30–45 minutes)

• C. Atracurium:

• Intermediate onset (2–3 minutes)
• Intermediate duration
• Eliminated by Hofmann degradation

• D. Rocuronium:

• Fastest onset among non-depolarizing muscle relaxants (60–90 seconds)
• Duration: 30–60 minutes
• Can be rapidly reversed with Sugammadex

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The maximum dose of Lidocaine (without adrenaline) for local anaesthesia is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4 mg/kg

The maximum recommended dose of lidocaine without adrenaline (epinephrine) for local anaesthesia is approximately 4 mg/kg.

• Without adrenaline: 4 mg/kg
• With adrenaline: up to 7 mg/kg

Adrenaline decreases systemic absorption of lidocaine, allowing a higher maximum dose.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The maximum safe dose for Lignocaine (without adrenaline) as a local anaesthetic drug is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 mg/kg

For Lignocaine (Lidocaine) as a local anaesthetic:

• Without adrenaline: maximum safe dose = 4.5 mg/kg (up to \~300 mg total)

• So here the best answer becomes 3mg/kg.

• With adrenaline: maximum safe dose = 7 mg/kg (adrenaline causes vasoconstriction, slowing systemic absorption, allowing a higher total dose)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which inhaled anaesthetic agent is preferred for paediatric induction of anaesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sevoflurane

Sevoflurane is preferred for paediatric induction because it has a non-pungent smell, causes minimal airway irritation, and provides rapid induction and smooth recovery. Desflurane and isoflurane are pungent and airway irritants, and halothane is avoided due to cardiac and hepatic risks.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following drug is used to reverse muscle relaxation induced by vecuronium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neostigmine

Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, reversed by increasing acetylcholine at the NMJ. Neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, achieves this and is routinely used with an anticholinergic (glycopyrrolate/atropine) to counter muscarinic effects. Succinylcholine is depolarizing and not used for reversal.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following true regarding benzodiazepines and barbiturates: 1. Both act on GABA-A chloride channel 2. Alcohol causes superadded CNS depression 3. Flumazenil reverses the action of both 4. Thiopentone has short duration of action due to its rapid metabolism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both 1 and 2 are correct

Benzodiazepines and barbiturates both act on the GABA-A chloride channel, and alcohol produces additive CNS depression with them.

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines only, not barbiturates, it is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors.

Thiopentone’s short action is due to redistribution, not rapid metabolism, it moves quickly from brain → muscle → fat.

Metabolism is actually slower. Therefore, statements 1 and 2 are correct.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of these is used for immediate reversal of Vecuronium in a patient for normal kidney function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sugammadex

Sugammadex reverses vecuronium by directly encapsulating the drug, producing rapid and complete recovery from neuromuscular blockade. It is the preferred agent for immediate reversal when renal function is normal; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are slower and ineffective for deep blockade.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of these statements is incorrect about Thiopentone?
options: It achieves maximum concentration in brain after IV infusion
Redistribution to adipose tissue and muscle is seen
The rapid decline in its effect is due to renal excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The rapid decline in its effect is due to renal excretion

Thiopentone is highly lipid soluble, causing rapid brain uptake immediately after IV dosing. Its effect terminates due to redistribution from the brain to muscle and adipose tissue—not renal excretion. Renal clearance contributes only to late drug elimination, not the rapid fall in anaesthetic effect. The rapid termination of action is due to redistribution, not elimination. Metabolism happens later in the liver, and renal excretion is not responsible for the immediate recovery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which one of the following is a nephrotoxic anaesthetic agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methoxyflurane

Methoxyflurane is the classic nephrotoxic inhalational anesthetic. It undergoes extensive metabolism, producing inorganic fluoride ions, which cause dose-dependent renal tubular toxicity, leading to polyuric renal failure.

Why not the other options?

• B. Isoflurane: Minimal metabolism; not nephrotoxic.
• C. Halothane: Associated with hepatotoxicity (halothane hepatitis), not nephrotoxicity.
• D. Nitrous oxide: Not nephrotoxic; prolonged exposure may cause vitamin B₁₂ deficiency.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 56-year-old female has been diagnosed with gallstones and is undergoing a preanaesthesia checkup. She has been a diabetic since the last 15 years, but sugar levels are within the limits. Which category of physical status does she fit into?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ASA II

The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative fitness and estimate perioperative risk.

ASA II — mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitations.

Quick reference for ASA-PS classification:

• ASA I — normal healthy patient
• ASA II — mild systemic disease, no functional limitation (e.g., well-controlled diabetes or hypertension, controlled asthma, current smoker, social alcohol use, obesity with BMI 30–40, mild lung disease)
• ASA III — severe systemic disease, some functional limitation (e.g., poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, diabetes with vascular complications, morbid obesity, active hepatitis, ESRD on dialysis)
• ASA IV — severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g., recent MI/CVA <3 months, ongoing cardiac ischemia, sepsis)
• ASA V — moribund, not expected to survive without surgery
• ASA VI — brain-dead patient for organ donation

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is scheduled for laparoscopic surgery under general anaesthesia in a day care setting. Which of the following factors makes him unsuitable for day care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes drive away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively

A mandatory requirement for day-care surgery is the presence of a responsible adult caregiver at home after discharge. Lack of an attendant is an absolute contraindication, making option C the correct factor that makes this patient unsuitable for ambulatory surgery.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient on long-term warfarin therapy is posted for surgery. What is the appropriate management?
options: Stop warfarin 5 days prior and switch to LMWH
Stop on the day of surgery
Stop warfarin 2 days before surgery without any bridging therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin 5 days prior and switch to LMWH

Patients receiving long-term warfarin who are undergoing major surgery should have warfarin discontinued approximately 5 days before surgery to allow the INR to normalize. In patients at high risk of thromboembolism (e.g., mechanical heart valves, atrial fibrillation with high stroke risk, recent venous thromboembolism), bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is recommended until shortly before surgery and restarted postoperatively when appropriate.

• Warfarin has a long half-life (36–42 hours).
• Stopping it 5 days before surgery usually reduces the INR to a safe level.
• LMWH bridging minimizes the period without anticoagulation in high-risk patients.

Why not the other options?

• B. Continue medication: Increases the risk of significant perioperative bleeding for most major surgeries.
• C. Stop on the day of surgery: Too late; the anticoagulant effect persists for several days.
• D. Stop warfarin 2 days before surgery without bridging therapy: Insufficient time for INR normalization and leaves high-risk patients inadequately managed.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with COPD is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. Which of the following preoperative measures is most effective in reducing the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Smoking cessation

Recognize that preoperative smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative pulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing elective surgery. Smoking cessation improves mucociliary clearance, reduces airway reactivity and sputum production, and enhances pulmonary function, particularly when stopped ≥4–8 weeks before surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Give antibiotics: Not indicated unless there is evidence of an active respiratory infection.
• B. Wait for 3 months: Routine postponement is not recommended; optimization, including smoking cessation, is more beneficial.
• D. Oxygen therapy: Corrects hypoxemia but does not reduce the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications in stable COPD patients.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Mallampati test is used for the assessment of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Airway

The Mallampati classification is a bedside airway assessment tool used to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation and identify patients at risk of a difficult airway. It assesses the visibility of the oropharyngeal structures when the patient opens the mouth maximally and protrudes the tongue without phonation.

• The Mallampati test assesses the airway by estimating the relationship between the tongue size and oropharyngeal space, thereby predicting the difficulty of laryngoscopy and intubation. ⭐

Why not the other options?

• A. Tongue size: The test indirectly reflects tongue size relative to the oral cavity but its purpose is airway assessment, not measuring tongue size.
• B. Ability to protrude jaw: Jaw protrusion is assessed by the Upper Lip Bite Test (ULBT), not the Mallampati test.
• C. Breath hold time: Breath-holding time is unrelated to the Mallampati classification.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following criteria corresponding to ASA grade III?
options: Severe illness which is constant threat to life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Severe illness

ASA III corresponds to severe systemic disease that limits activity but is not a constant threat to life. The disease is significant and limits activity, but not actively life threatening at rest. It is more serious than mild or moderate illness but not as critical as ASA IV, where disease poses a continual threat.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following parameters are assessed during preoperative airway assessment for a surgical patient? 1. Mouth opening 2. Ability to protrude the jaw 3. Thyromental distance 4. Cervicomental distance Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The important parameters in preoperative airway assessment include:

1. Mouth opening — Correct

• Adequate mouth opening is essential for laryngoscope insertion and airway manipulation.
• An inter-incisor distance >3 cm is generally considered favorable.

2. Ability to protrude the jaw — Correct

• Assesses mandibular mobility and predicts difficulty in aligning the airway axes.
• Inability to protrude the lower incisors beyond the upper incisors suggests a potentially difficult airway.

3. Thyromental distance — Correct

• Measured from the thyroid notch to the mentum with the neck extended.
• A distance <6–6.5 cm suggests a potentially difficult intubation.

4. Cervicomental distance — Incorrect

• It is not a standard parameter used in routine preoperative airway assessment.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 35-year-old man undergoes an interscalene brachial plexus block for upper limb surgery. Soon after the procedure, he develops ipsilateral ptosis and miosis, which resolve within a few hours. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stellate ganglion block

• The patient has Horner syndrome, characterized by:

• Ptosis
• Miosis
• Anhidrosis (may be present)

• During an interscalene brachial plexus block, local anesthetic may spread to the stellate ganglion (cervicothoracic sympathetic ganglion).
• Temporary blockade of the cervical sympathetic chain produces Horner syndrome.
• The condition is usually transient and resolves as the anesthetic wears off.
• It does not indicate nerve injury.
• Recurrent laryngeal nerve block causes hoarseness.
• Phrenic nerve block causes ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.
• Facial nerve block produces facial weakness rather than miosis or ptosis.

High-yield complications of interscalene block

• Phrenic nerve block → Hemidiaphragmatic paralysis
• Recurrent laryngeal nerve block → Hoarseness
• Stellate ganglion block → Horner syndrome
• Intravascular injection → Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60 years old male patient was undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the surgery, it was observed that there was a sudden decrease in etCO2 to 8 mm Hg, SpO2 was 90%, BP dropped to 80/50 mm Hg and peak airway pressure was observed to be 18 mm Hg. Which of the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CO2 embolism

A sudden sharp fall in EtCO₂, hypotension, mild desaturation, and normal airway pressures during laparoscopy strongly point to CO₂ embolism. Pneumothorax, bronchospasm, and endobronchial intubation all increase airway pressures, which is not seen here. CO₂ embolism is a known complication of pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing parotid gland surgery. Ten minutes into the surgery, the end-tidal CO₂ increases, along with a temperature of 104°F, heart rate of 140 bpm, and blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malignant hyperthermia

Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane) or succinylcholine. It is characterized by a hypermetabolic state, with the earliest and most sensitive sign being a rapid rise in end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂), followed by hyperthermia, tachycardia, muscle rigidity, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalemia.

• The patient develops sudden increase in ETCO₂, temperature of 104°F, tachycardia, and hypertension shortly after induction of anesthesia—findings that are classic for malignant hyperthermia.

Why not the other options?

• B. Heat stroke: Caused by environmental heat exposure and is not associated with anesthesia or an early rise in ETCO₂.
• C. Heat exhaustion: Presents with dehydration and mild hyperthermia, without severe hypermetabolism or marked ETCO₂ elevation.
• D. Heat syncope: Transient loss of consciousness due to peripheral vasodilation; does not cause hyperthermia or increased ETCO₂.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery is administered succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Shortly after administration, he develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene sodium

• Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder triggered by succinylcholine and volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane). It is caused by a mutation in the RYR1 (ryanodine receptor), leading to uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, resulting in sustained muscle contraction and a hypermetabolic state.
• The drug of choice for treatment is intravenous dantrolene sodium, which inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Why not the other options?

• A. Neostigmine: Reverses non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers; ineffective in malignant hyperthermia.
• C. Atropine: Used for bradycardia or to reduce secretions; no role in MH.
• D. Midazolam: Provides sedation but does not treat the underlying pathophysiology.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with a humerus fracture is scheduled for orthopaedic surgery. Regional anaesthesia is planned, and a brachial plexus block is performed. Through which approach is the brachial plexus most commonly accessed for this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supraclavicular

The supraclavicular approach to the brachial plexus provides the most complete and reliable anesthesia of the upper limb below the shoulder. Because the plexus is densely packed at the level of the trunks/divisions, it is commonly used for orthopedic procedures involving the humerus, elbow, forearm, and hand.

The patient requires orthopedic surgery for a humerus fracture. A supraclavicular brachial plexus block offers:

• Rapid onset
• Dense sensory and motor blockade
• Excellent anesthesia for surgery involving the upper extremity below the shoulder

Why not the other options?

• B. Infraclavicular: Primarily blocks the cords; useful for elbow, forearm, and hand surgery but less commonly used for proximal humeral procedures.
• C. Interscalene: Best for shoulder and proximal humerus surgery, but often spares the ulnar nerve (C8–T1) and is not ideal for surgery involving the distal upper limb.
• D. Axillary: Suitable for forearm and hand surgery; does not reliably anesthetize the musculocutaneous nerve unless blocked separately and is inadequate for humeral fractures.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A person has suffered from chest trauma resulting in fracture of 2-6th ribs. He is being given pain relief by IV analgesic agents. Which of these blocks will be helpful in pain relief?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic epidural

Rib fractures from T2–T6 produce severe chest wall pain best relieved by thoracic epidural, which provides segmental analgesia to the corresponding dermatomes. Cervical and supraclavicular blocks do not cover thoracic levels, and lumbar epidural is too low to provide effective analgesia for upper thoracic ribs.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the statements is true about lumbar puncture? 1. LP is urgently indicated if CT scan is negative in suspected SAH 2. Post dural puncture head ache is common in females and older adults 3. Meningitis after LP is an unusual side effect 4. LP is safely done in thrombocytopenia more than 10000
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3

• LP is indicated after a negative CT in suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage to detect xanthochromia (true).
• Meningitis is a rare complication (true).
• PDPH is more common in young females, not older adults, and LP is unsafe at platelet counts around 10,000 (requires ≥50,000). Hence only statements 1 and 3 are correct.
